modules.summary: Connect one tested calculation to a publisher/subscriber boundary.
modules.why: ROS 2 becomes useful when it connects understood components rather than hiding unfamiliar code behind a launch command.
explanation: A ROS 2 node is a unit of computation that communicates through interfaces such as topics, services, and actions. For a first integration, keep the engineering calculation in an ordinary tested C++ library and use a node as the adapter that receives a message, checks its meaning, calls the library, and publishes a result. This keeps framework learning from replacing ordinary software reasoning.

A message contract includes more than field types. State units, coordinate frames when relevant, timestamp meaning, validity, expected rate, and what happens when messages disappear. Matching a topic name does not guarantee matching meaning. Quality-of-service settings affect delivery behavior, and endpoints need compatible settings to communicate. Use documentation for the installed ROS distribution instead of assuming examples from another release are interchangeable.

An executor schedules callbacks; callback groups and executor choices affect concurrency. Do not assume that a callback's code is automatically isolated from every other callback or that timers imply hard-real-time deadlines. Start with one simple topic and one deterministic fixture, inspect what is actually received, and then test missing, delayed, and duplicate messages. This lesson defines the integration task; use the official installed-distribution tutorial for exact package and build commands.

example.explanation: This framework-independent adapter policy can be tested before binding it to a ROS message. It assumes timestamps share a meaningful clock and requires separate finite-value validation.

walkthrough: Complete an official publisher/subscriber tutorial for your installed distribution.
Write a message contract beside the interface definition.
Call a tested library from the callback.
Replay fresh, stale, missing, and duplicate data and record the observed policy.
pitfalls: Matching field types does not establish matching units or coordinate frames.
Incompatible QoS can prevent communication even when topic names match.
A timer callback is not by itself a hard-real-time guarantee.

exercises.title: Contract age check
exercises.prompt: Apply should_process to valid measurements with three ages.
hints: A false validity flag overrides age.
exercises.solution: The function accepts age from zero through 0.5; older messages do not enter the calculation.
exercises.extension: Add finiteness checks.

exercises.title: Document a topic
exercises.prompt: Write a contract for a simulated temperature topic with a timestamp and quality flag.
exercises.expected: Units, clock, expected rate, validity, and missing-data policy are explicit
hints: Avoid a bare field named value.
Choose a timeout policy that is a learning assumption.
exercises.solution: A complete contract states Celsius, the simulated shared clock, nominal update rate, how quality is encoded, and how absence is reported.
tests: Consumer rejects the wrong unit convention at its adapter boundary.
Missing messages produce the documented state.
exercises.extension: Version the interface when meaning changes.

exercises.title: Replay before hardware
exercises.prompt: Feed a node a saved sequence containing valid, stale, duplicate, and absent intervals.
exercises.inputs: Sequence IDs 1,2,2,4 with a long gap before 4
exercises.expected: Logged decisions explain every accepted or rejected record
hints: A duplicate policy must be chosen.
exercises.solution: Separate freshness and duplicate checks; report the long interval as missing-data evidence rather than inventing sample 3.
tests: Replaying the fixture gives the same decisions.
exercises.extension: Compare the node output with the pure library tests.

exercises.title: Silent subscriber
exercises.prompt: A subscriber receives nothing despite matching topic names. Build a focused diagnosis.
exercises.inputs: Publisher exists; types and QoS not yet checked
exercises.expected: Verify discovery, type, QoS compatibility, and callback execution
hints: Do not immediately rewrite the calculation.
exercises.solution: Confirm both endpoints are in the intended domain, have matching message types and compatible QoS, and that the subscriber executor is running.
tests: The node logs a callback when a fixture arrives.
exercises.extension: Document the actual installed distribution and chosen QoS.

review.question: Where should reusable math live?
review.answer: In a framework-independent library with tests; the node adapts messages and policy.

review.question: What else matters besides a topic name?
review.answer: Message type, semantic contract, discovery context, QoS compatibility, and executing callbacks.

modules.title: From prototype to a reviewable engineering component
modules.summary: Package a small component with requirements, tests, limitations, and a reproducible demonstration.
modules.why: A portfolio becomes credible when another person can rebuild the result and see what it does under failure.
explanation: A useful engineering component has a bounded purpose. Write a short statement such as classify a simulated temperature record as fresh, stale, or invalid, and list what lies outside scope. Connect each requirement to at least one test or demonstration. This traceability is not bureaucracy for its own sake: it makes gaps visible when a feature changes or a new collaborator asks why the program behaves a certain way.

Preserve evidence, not only screenshots. Include source, build instructions, a small data fixture, expected outputs, tests, and a concise explanation of assumptions. Record the compiler and relevant library versions used for the demonstration. Separate measured observations from guarantees; a desktop timing plot and a successful replay are valuable, but neither certifies flight suitability or safe operation of a real mechanism.

Study mature systems after you can explain a small one. F Prime provides examples of component-oriented flight-software architecture, commands, telemetry, and testing. NASA cFS is a separate ecosystem centered on reusable flight-software services and applications. Reading them can reveal ideas to borrow, but copying a framework into a project does not transfer mission qualification. Your next step should answer one concrete learning question, not simply increase the stack.

example.explanation: This small trace table illustrates a documentation relationship. A real project may keep it in Markdown or a test-management format.

walkthrough: Choose one component with a narrow, explainable purpose.
Map requirements to tests and example outputs.
Perform a clean build and demonstration using only the README.
Write limitations and a next experiment before adding another dependency.
pitfalls: Framework adoption does not confer flight qualification.
A video without reproducible inputs is weak evidence of behavior.
A portfolio should distinguish your authored code from dependencies and generated code.

exercises.title: Requirement with a boundary
exercises.prompt: Rewrite reject old data as a testable requirement.
exercises.inputs: A chosen learning threshold of 0.5 s
exercises.expected: Reject age > 0.5 s; define equality and future timestamps
exercises.solution: A precise requirement identifies the clock assumption, strictness, output status, and test at 0.5 versus 0.5001 seconds.
exercises.extension: Record why the threshold was chosen for the simulation.

exercises.title: Evidence manifest
exercises.prompt: List the smallest files needed to reproduce a telemetry decision component.
exercises.inputs: Source, build, tests, fixture, expected result
exercises.expected: A new folder can reproduce the demonstration
hints: Do not rely on an old binary.
exercises.solution: Package authored code, CMake recipe, test executable source, input fixture, expected output, and README with assumptions and limitations.
exercises.extension: Add a machine-readable result summary.

exercises.title: Framework reading expedition
exercises.prompt: Read one F Prime tutorial and identify the equivalents of input, state, output, and test.
exercises.expected: A one-page map connecting a tutorial to your component
hints: Use framework terms only when you can define them.
exercises.solution: Map a command or port to input, component fields to state, telemetry/events to observations, and test harnesses to evidence.
tests: Every mapped element cites a source section.
Mark unknown concepts for later study.
exercises.extension: Implement one tiny tutorial only after the map makes sense.

exercises.title: Overstated portfolio claim
exercises.prompt: A README says flight-ready because it uses C++ and passes tests. Rewrite it accurately.
exercises.inputs: Desktop simulation and selected tests only
exercises.expected: A tested educational prototype with explicit coverage and limitations
exercises.solution: State the tested scenarios, platform, known gaps, and absence of operational qualification. The result can be impressive without unsupported guarantees.
tests: Limitations include untested hardware and timing assumptions.
exercises.extension: Add a risk-driven next-test list.

review.question: What makes a requirement reviewable?
review.answer: It is specific enough to connect to observable evidence and clear boundary behavior.

review.question: Why read mature frameworks later?
review.answer: You can connect their abstractions to problems you already understand instead of collecting unfamiliar machinery.

modules.title: A calculation you can rerun
modules.summary: Turn a hand calculation into a transparent script with named quantities and units.
modules.why: An engineering result is useful only when you can reconstruct where it came from. A small repeatable script is your first laboratory notebook.
explanation: Begin with a question small enough to solve on paper: how much electrical energy does a 12 W instrument use in 15 minutes? Name power and duration, convert minutes to seconds, multiply, and label the answer. A variable name such as duration_s records an assumption that a bare number cannot. MATLAB will happily multiply incompatible quantities; dimensional consistency is your responsibility until you deliberately introduce a units system.

A script records the sequence that produces your result. The Command Window is excellent for experiments, but commands that worked only because yesterday’s variables still existed are not a reproducible analysis. Put every required input in the script, run it from the beginning, and change just one input. A semicolon suppresses display; it does not skip computation. Comments should explain a physical assumption or choice, not repeat an obvious assignment.

Keep a small evidence trail beside the code: the question, input units, one hand calculation, and the expected behavior when an input doubles. Here doubling power should double energy. Do not let output formatting imply more measurement accuracy than you possess. The computer can print many digits even when your power estimate is approximate. This habit becomes valuable later when a long thermal model contains thousands of operations and only a few independent checks.

example.explanation: The answer is 10800 J. Watts are joules per second, so the seconds cancel in the multiplication.

walkthrough: Calculate the answer on paper before running the script.
Save energy_budget.m with all inputs at the top.
Run from the first line, then double power and predict the result.
Record why joules and watt-hours are different numerical representations of the same energy.
pitfalls: Typing 15 as seconds when the problem says minutes.
Using ans as a lasting variable instead of naming the quantity.
Treating displayed precision as sensor accuracy.

exercises.title: Instrument energy
exercises.prompt: Calculate the energy consumed by an 8 W sensor over 30 minutes. Print joules and watt-hours.
exercises.solution: duration_s=30*60; energy_j=8*duration_s; energy_wh=energy_j/3600. Multiplying 8 W by 0.5 h provides an independent check.
tests: Doubling duration returns twice the energy.
exercises.extension: Add a second instrument and compare separate versus combined energy.

exercises.title: Battery estimate with assumptions
exercises.prompt: Estimate ideal runtime from a 40 Wh battery powering a constant 10 W load. State one reason the real runtime might differ.
exercises.expected: 4 h; the estimate ignores conversion losses and changing load.
hints: Do not mix Wh with seconds.
exercises.solution: runtime_h=40/10. This is a simplified energy balance, not a battery performance guarantee.
tests: A zero load must be handled explicitly, not reported as ordinary finite runtime.
exercises.extension: Represent an assumed 80% usable fraction as a named input.

exercises.title: A unit audit
exercises.prompt: A script computes energy_j=power_w*duration_min. Explain the error and make the input interface harder to misuse.
exercises.expected: Correct energy is 600 J, not 10 J.
hints: Write the units under each factor.
Convert at the boundary of the calculation.
exercises.solution: Convert duration_min to duration_s=60*duration_min, then multiply. Keep the conversion visible and label outputs.
exercises.extension: Write a short input/output contract for the script.

exercises.title: The stale variable
exercises.prompt: A script contains only energy_j=power_w*60 and works once, then fails in a fresh workspace. Diagnose and repair it.
exercises.inputs: power_w happened to exist from an earlier session.
exercises.expected: A self-contained script assigns or receives power_w before use.
hints: Inspect the script, not only the workspace.
Ask what an independent reader needs.
exercises.solution: The script has an undeclared dependency. Put the intended power value in the input section and explain the one-minute duration.
tests: Change the input and rerun from the beginning.
exercises.extension: Identify another analysis habit that can hide state.

review.question: What does a semicolon change?
review.answer: It suppresses ordinary display of that statement’s result; the calculation still occurs.

review.question: Why include units in a variable name?
review.answer: It makes the intended representation visible and helps catch conversion mistakes; it does not enforce units automatically.

modules.title: Vectors, indexing, and sample identity
modules.summary: Represent several measurements without losing which sample each value belongs to.
modules.why: Sensor logs are sequences, not isolated scalars. Indexing mistakes can pair a correct measurement with the wrong time.
explanation: A vector lets you give one name to a sequence of samples. Decide what an element represents before performing an operation: a temperature, a time, a channel, or a trial. MATLAB indexing starts at one. The first reading in a three-element vector is reading(1), and the final one is reading(end). A row vector and a column vector contain similar-looking numbers but have different shapes, which matters when you combine them.

Treat the time and value arrays as a pair. If you remove the second temperature but keep the second timestamp, every later interpretation can become wrong. Build an index selection once and apply it consistently to both arrays. A logical mask names a property of the samples, such as readings above a review threshold. It is often easier to inspect that mask than a loop containing several nested conditions.

Before trusting a selection, write down the expected indices using a tiny dataset. Include a reading exactly equal to the threshold so that the distinction between greater-than and greater-than-or-equal is deliberate. Missing samples are not automatically zero, and an empty selection is a legitimate outcome. Your future rover may produce no readings meeting a condition; the analysis should report that clearly instead of inventing an average.

example.explanation: Only the final sample exceeds 30 °C, so review_times_s is 6.

walkthrough: Create four timestamps and four readings on paper.
Inspect size, numel, first, and last elements.
Build one mask and apply it to both arrays.
Test a boundary value and a mask selecting no samples.
pitfalls: Starting indices at zero.
Filtering values but forgetting their timestamps.
Confusing an empty vector with a zero measurement.

exercises.title: Choose the samples
exercises.prompt: Select the first and third readings, then select the last two.
hints: end refers to the last index.
exercises.solution: x([1 3]) selects [12 18]; x(end-1:end) selects [18 21].
tests: The last-two result contains exactly two elements.
exercises.extension: Repeat with a column vector and describe the output shape.

exercises.title: Find threshold times
exercises.prompt: Report the times where voltage is strictly below 11.5 V.
exercises.solution: The mask is [false false true false]. The equal-to-threshold reading is not selected.
tests: All values above the threshold produces empty output.
exercises.extension: Return the matching voltages alongside their times.

exercises.title: Keep paired data aligned
exercises.prompt: Remove invalid negative distances while preserving the matching trial identifiers.
hints: Zero distance is valid under this contract.
Use the same mask for both vectors.
exercises.solution: valid=distance_m>=0; trial=trial(valid); distance_m=distance_m(valid). State whether missing values require a different check.
tests: The retained arrays have the same length.
exercises.extension: Add an explicit NaN value and decide a finite-data policy.

exercises.title: The shifted clock
exercises.prompt: A program deletes value(2) after a sensor fault but leaves time unchanged, then plots them. Explain both the obvious and the subtle failure.
exercises.expected: Use one validity mask; retained pairs are (0,10),(2,12).
hints: Padding or trimming to match lengths does not restore identity.
exercises.solution: Mask both arrays together. Merely truncating time to two samples would silently attach 12 to t=1.
tests: The second valid reading remains at t=2.
exercises.extension: Store paired data in a table in a later module.

review.question: What is the difference between numel and size?
review.answer: numel counts all elements; size reports the dimensions that describe their arrangement.

review.question: Why reuse a logical mask?
review.answer: It preserves sample alignment across all variables filtered by the same validity decision.

modules.title: Array operations and matrix meaning
modules.summary: Choose operators by the mathematics you intend rather than by which one avoids an error.
modules.why: The same symbols can mean a per-sample calculation or a linear transformation. Aerospace calculations use both.
explanation: Suppose you have several measured speeds and want their squares. Each speed should be squared independently, so use .^2. If you instead have a matrix representing a transformation, multiplying that matrix by itself has a different mathematical meaning. The dot in an operator is a statement about the operation, not a cosmetic syntax fix. Write one small result by hand before applying an unfamiliar operator to a large array.

Shape is part of the contract. Two row vectors can be combined element by element. A row vector and a column vector can produce an entire grid through implicit expansion. That feature is useful for parameter sweeps, but it can also turn an intended four-sample result into a four-by-four matrix without an error. Inspect size before and after important operations and explain the meaning of each output dimension.

In this module you need multiplication, powers, and basic matrix multiplication; advanced linear algebra can come later. Think of a matrix-vector product as weighted combinations of inputs. For example, two simple sensor combinations can be represented by two rows. Do not memorize a blanket rule to put dots everywhere: that would break genuine matrix equations. Your goal is to recognize whether corresponding samples or coupled variables are being combined.

example.explanation: The energies are [1 4 9] J for a 2 kg mass. The independent matrix example returns [4;2].

walkthrough: Compute the three energy values by hand.
Compare size(speed_mps) with size(speed_mps').
Predict a 2-by-2 matrix-vector product.
Write a comment explaining the mathematical role of each dot operator.
pitfalls: Using ^ when a vector needs element-wise powers.
Assuming implicit expansion always matches the intended sample pairing.
Replacing matrix multiplication with .* just to silence an error.

exercises.title: Square each speed
exercises.prompt: Calculate one-half mass times speed squared for each sample.
exercises.solution: energy_j=0.5*mass_kg.*speed_mps.^2. Each output belongs to the corresponding speed sample.
tests: At zero speed energy is zero.
Doubling speed multiplies energy by four.
exercises.extension: Plot energy against speed with units.

exercises.title: Read a transformation
exercises.prompt: Compute the two weighted sensor combinations represented by A*x.
hints: The first output uses the first row.
exercises.solution: Matrix multiplication combines rows with the input column. A.*x would express a different operation.
exercises.extension: Describe each row as a plain-language formula.

exercises.title: Intentional parameter grid
exercises.prompt: Create energies for masses [1;2] kg and speeds [1 2 3] m/s using implicit expansion, then explain the axes.
exercises.solution: 0.5*mass.*speed.^2 forms all mass-speed combinations. This is a grid, not two paired records.
tests: Second row is twice the first.
exercises.extension: Add row and column labels before exporting the grid.

exercises.title: The accidental grid
exercises.prompt: A calculation intended three paired products but returned a 3-by-3 array. Repair the representation.
exercises.expected: Paired products [10 40 90], if a row output is chosen.
exercises.solution: Use a.*b.' or convert both to columns with a(:).*b(:). The original expanded every combination.
exercises.extension: Add a shape assertion before multiplying.

review.question: When is .* appropriate?
review.answer: When the intended mathematics multiplies corresponding elements or deliberately expanded combinations.

review.question: Why can a shape error produce no exception?
review.answer: Implicit expansion can make mismatched orientations mathematically compatible while still violating the intended data contract.

modules.title: Plots that support a claim
modules.summary: Make figures that preserve units, sampling, and uncertainty rather than simply looking smooth.
modules.why: A plot is often the first thing a project reviewer sees. It should make the evidence easier to evaluate.
explanation: A line plot joins your supplied points; it does not prove that the physical system followed a straight line between them. Markers reveal where data actually exists. Before plotting, ask what claim the figure should support: a temperature rose, two runs differ, or a model misses a transient. Choose axes and labels that let a reader test that claim. Use seconds, degrees Celsius, volts, or other explicit units rather than relying on a caption remembered from class.

Keep comparisons fair. Two runs shown on different scales can look deceptively similar. Plot them together when appropriate and distinguish them using markers or line styles as well as color. When time grids differ, do not silently treat sample index as time. Show each run on its actual timestamps, and label invented data as invented. Save the code that produced the figure so a corrected measurement can regenerate it.

Visual polish should follow data checks. Inspect vector lengths, order, missing values, and bounds before adjusting colors. A jagged line may expose a real problem worth investigating, while smoothing may hide it. For a small lesson dataset, calculate one plotted point independently. For a later report, include the data source, processing decisions, and limitations. This turns a picture into a reproducible piece of engineering evidence.

example.explanation: Markers expose the four sample times. The line is a visual connection, not an independently validated continuous model.

walkthrough: Write the intended claim in one sentence.
Plot original data with markers and labeled units.
Add a second run using the same axes.
Check one point and document any filtering.
pitfalls: Plotting sample indices while labeling the axis as seconds.
Using a legend that does not match series order.
Removing inconvenient points without recording a reason.

exercises.title: Label a warm-up
exercises.prompt: Plot the given temperatures against actual time and show sample markers.
hints: Use a marker style such as o-.
exercises.solution: plot(t_s,T_c,"o-"); xlabel("Time (s)"); ylabel("Temperature (°C)"). The unequal spacing must remain visible.
exercises.extension: Explain what is unknown between samples.

exercises.title: Compare two runs
exercises.prompt: Show both runs on common axes with a meaningful legend.
exercises.expected: At t=2, A is 1 °C warmer than B.
exercises.solution: plot(t,runA,"o-",t,runB,"s--"); legend("Run A","Run B"); add units. The claim concerns these samples only.
exercises.extension: Add a difference plot on a separate axis.

exercises.title: Model residual figure
exercises.prompt: Plot measured-minus-predicted residuals and identify whether the model is consistently low.
exercises.expected: Residuals [0 1 2] °C; prediction is low at the latter two samples.
exercises.solution: residual=measured-predicted. The increasing residual suggests an error pattern worth investigating, not proof of a particular cause.
tests: Swapping subtraction reverses the sign and requires relabeling.
exercises.extension: Describe two model assumptions that could be tested next.

exercises.title: The wrong clock label
exercises.prompt: A chart uses plot(T) and xlabel("Time (s)") although samples were collected every ten seconds starting at zero. Repair it.
hints: The default x values are indices.
exercises.solution: t=(0:numel(T)-1)*10; plot(t,T,"o-"). Without this correction the plot misstates both origin and duration.
exercises.extension: Handle an irregular time vector.

review.question: What does a marker contribute?
review.answer: It identifies actual supplied samples rather than letting a connecting line imply continuous observation.

review.question: Why save plotting code?
review.answer: It records how data became a figure and lets corrected inputs regenerate the same analysis.

modules.title: Functions and input contracts
modules.summary: Package a calculation so its inputs, outputs, and assumptions are explicit.
modules.why: A thermal equation reused across several scripts should have one tested implementation, not five slightly different copies.
explanation: A function makes a boundary around a calculation. Inputs cross into it, outputs come back, and local intermediate values stay inside. That boundary gives you a place to state units, valid ranges, and array shapes. Start with a scalar conversion rather than a large simulation. Decide whether the function accepts one number, a vector, or both before writing the body.

Validation is not decoration. A cooling time constant must be positive, and a measured duration should not silently become complex or infinite. Reject inputs that do not belong to the intended model. Conversely, do not invent an unnecessary restriction just because the first example used a positive temperature: negative Celsius temperatures are physically ordinary. The contract should follow the quantity, not a convenient example.

Keep numerical work separate from presentation. A function returning energy can be tested without opening a figure or reading a file. Another script can gather inputs and plot the result. This separation makes homework easier to debug and later lets a batch of simulation runs call the same model. Use a function file matching the function name, include a short help comment, and test a known value before making the interface broader.

example.explanation: Save as celsius_to_kelvin.m. The validation permits negative Celsius values above absolute zero.

walkthrough: Write the input/output contract before the implementation.
Save one function with the matching filename.
Call it with a normal value and a boundary value.
Test a deliberately invalid value and read the diagnostic.
pitfalls: Relying on a variable that exists only in the calling workspace.
Rejecting all negative Celsius values.
Mixing plots, files, and a simple numerical calculation in one function.

exercises.title: Conversion function
exercises.prompt: Write a function converting minutes to seconds for nonnegative finite numeric input.
hints: Multiplication by 60 works on an array.
Validate the whole input, not only its first element.
exercises.solution: Return minutes*60 after checking finite real nonnegative values. Use a name that includes the direction of conversion.
exercises.extension: Document whether an empty input is accepted.

exercises.title: Energy interface
exercises.prompt: Write energy_j(power_w,duration_s) for scalar nonnegative finite inputs. Keep printing outside it.
hints: A return value is easier to test than a printed sentence.
exercises.solution: The function checks scalar size and range, then returns power_w*duration_s. The caller labels the result.
tests: A vector is rejected under this contract.
exercises.extension: Extend deliberately to equal-sized arrays.

exercises.title: Cooling contract
exercises.prompt: Design the input checks for T=Ta+(T0-Ta)*exp(-t/tau), accepting vector t and scalar parameters.
hints: t must be nonnegative; temperatures can be negative.
exercises.solution: Validate real finite values, positive scalar tau, scalar temperatures, and nonnegative t. Return an array with t’s shape.
exercises.extension: Add help text explaining the lumped-model assumption.

exercises.title: Invisible dependency
exercises.prompt: A function accepts duration_s but refers to power_w without an input or local assignment. It worked as a script. Repair its design.
exercises.expected: power_w must become an explicit input.
hints: Do not repair this with a global variable.
exercises.solution: Use function E=energy(power_w,duration_s). Call energy(12,20), then test 240 J.
tests: Calling with documented inputs works in a fresh session.
Changing caller variable names does not change the function.
exercises.extension: Find another hidden assumption and move it into the contract.

review.question: Why keep plotting outside a small model function?
review.answer: It makes the numerical result independently testable and reusable in other interfaces.

review.question: What belongs in an input contract?
review.answer: Units, types, sizes, valid ranges, missing-data policy, and the meaning of each output.

modules.title: Importing logs without trusting them blindly
modules.summary: Read a table, inspect its schema, and make missing-data decisions visible.
modules.why: Real experimental logs contain empty cells, inconsistent units, duplicate times, and malformed values. Import success does not mean scientific validity.
explanation: A table attaches names to columns and keeps related measurements together. That is useful for a log containing time, temperature, and operating mode. Read the file, then inspect the variable names, types, and a few rows before applying a formula. A column that looks numeric in a spreadsheet may arrive as text because one row contains a unit suffix or a status word.

Define the data contract before cleaning. Is time measured in seconds from the start or represented by calendar timestamps? Can two measurements have the same time? Does a blank mean missing, zero, or not applicable? Retain the original file and construct a separate validity mask or cleaned table. Record how many rows were excluded and why; the removal itself can affect your conclusion.

Use synthetic files to test the importer before relying on an expensive experiment. Include one normal row, one missing value, one duplicate time, and one out-of-order row. Decide whether to reject, retain with a flag, or sort each case. Sorting is not automatically harmless because it can hide a logging-order problem. An honest report distinguishes what the instrument measured from what the analysis inferred or repaired.

example.explanation: The example checks expected column names and removes nonfinite numeric rows into a new table; inspect imported types before using it.

walkthrough: Create a tiny CSV with explicit column names.
Inspect imported types and verify the expected columns.
Build a documented validity mask.
Keep raw and cleaned data separate and report exclusions.
pitfalls: Treating missing temperature as zero.
Assuming automatic type detection always matches the intended schema.
Sorting or deleting rows without leaving a record.

exercises.title: Read a tiny CSV
exercises.prompt: Create a three-row CSV in a scratch folder, import it, and report row count and column names.
exercises.solution: readtable reads the file; height(T) gives three. Confirm both columns are numeric and names match the contract.
exercises.extension: Add an operating-mode text column.

exercises.title: Missing measurement audit
exercises.prompt: Keep finite temperatures and count missing rows without changing the original table.
hints: Select complete rows with the mask.
exercises.solution: valid=isfinite(T.temperature_c); clean=T(valid,:); excluded=sum(~valid). This does not invent a temperature at t=1.
tests: The gap at 1 s remains visible.
exercises.extension: Plot the gap instead of joining across it automatically.

exercises.title: Timestamp policy
exercises.prompt: Specify and implement a check for strictly increasing time. Explain what you would do with a violation.
exercises.expected: The duplicate at the third row violates strict increase.
hints: A zero difference is not positive.
exercises.solution: all(diff(time_s)>0) is false. Return a diagnostic with the offending row pair; do not silently average duplicate readings without a stated rule.
exercises.extension: Separate duplicate and reverse-order diagnostics.

exercises.title: A missing value becomes ice
exercises.prompt: A cleaning script replaces NaN temperature with 0 before averaging. Diagnose the scientific error.
exercises.expected: Known-data mean is 21 °C; zero substitution produces 14 °C.
hints: State the denominator used in the average.
exercises.solution: Retain missingness, report two valid observations and one missing, and compute the mean only under an explicit known-data policy.
tests: An all-missing set reports no estimate.
exercises.extension: Explain why interpolation also requires assumptions.

review.question: Why retain the raw file?
review.answer: It preserves evidence and allows cleaning choices to be audited or revised.

review.question: What should accompany a cleaned-data result?
review.answer: The validity policy, number and reasons for excluded records, units, and any interpolation or sorting decisions.

modules.title: Tests, tolerances, and useful failures
modules.summary: Turn physical expectations and edge cases into small repeatable tests.
modules.why: A simulation may run without crashing while returning the wrong answer. Tests give correctness a visible definition.
explanation: Start with a case whose result you know independently. A zero-duration energy calculation should return zero. A cooling model at its initial time should return the initial temperature. These are stronger tests than merely repeating the implementation’s formula in a second place. Include one ordinary value, one boundary, and one invalid input so the interface is tested as well as the arithmetic.

Floating-point calculations often need tolerances. An absolute tolerance measures an acceptable error in the output’s units; a relative tolerance scales with the reference magnitude. Neither should be chosen only to make a failing test pass. Near zero, relative error alone is awkward. State the reason for a tolerance and keep measurement uncertainty distinct from numerical rounding: they are different questions.

A failing test is useful information. Reduce the input to the smallest example that still fails, inspect intermediate quantities, and identify which assumption broke. Assertions can document invariants while developing a script, and larger projects can grow into MATLAB’s testing framework. Keep tests runnable without clicking through figures or requiring private files. A future version of you should be able to reproduce a failure with one clear command.

example.explanation: The second comparison allows tiny representation error instead of demanding exact equality of decimal arithmetic.

walkthrough: Choose an independent known result.
Write normal, boundary, and invalid-input cases.
State an absolute or relative tolerance with units.
Deliberately break the model and confirm a test detects it.
pitfalls: Comparing every floating-point value with exact equality.
Using a huge tolerance to hide a modeling error.
Testing the same formula against an identical copy of itself.

exercises.title: Boundary test
exercises.prompt: Write tests for a minutes-to-seconds conversion at 0, 1, and 2.5 minutes.
exercises.expected: All three pass; a mistaken factor of 100 fails.
hints: Select values with simple independent answers.
exercises.solution: Use assert on the known outputs. Integer and half-minute cases make the conversion mistake obvious.
exercises.extension: Test a negative input rejection.

exercises.title: Mixed tolerance
exercises.prompt: Write a comparison using abs(actual-reference)<=atol+rtol*abs(reference).
exercises.expected: Pass, since 0.001 is less than about 0.010001.
exercises.solution: allowed=atol+rtol*abs(reference); compare absolute error with allowed. Document why these tolerances fit the problem.
tests: A zero reference is governed by atol.
exercises.extension: Use a different tolerance for a quantity measured in millimeters.

exercises.title: Physical invariant
exercises.prompt: Design three model tests for passive cooling toward a constant ambient with positive time constant.
exercises.expected: Initial value 40; values remain between 20 and 40; temperature decreases.
exercises.solution: Check T(0)=40 within tolerance, all T>=20 and T<=40, and diff(T)<=small_tolerance. These verify model properties independently of a chosen output vector.
tests: Equal initial and ambient temperatures stay constant.
exercises.extension: Explain why these tests still do not validate real hardware.

exercises.title: Tolerance hides a unit error
exercises.prompt: A result of 240000 is accepted against reference 240 using atol=1e6. Diagnose the test and model.
exercises.inputs: Power was entered in milliwatts but treated as watts.
exercises.expected: Correct output is 240 J; the error is 1000-fold.
hints: Check input units before changing tolerances.
A passing test is only as meaningful as its acceptance rule.
exercises.solution: Convert milliwatts to watts and choose tolerance based on the intended numerical calculation. Keep a known unit-conversion test.
exercises.extension: Add a test documenting the input unit.

review.question: What is an invariant?
review.answer: A property expected to remain true across a range of valid inputs, such as a conserved total or a bounded passive response.

review.question: Why is numerical tolerance different from measurement uncertainty?
review.answer: Tolerance checks computation against a reference; uncertainty describes incomplete knowledge of the physical input or observation.

modules.title: Linear systems and residuals
modules.summary: Solve coupled equations and check whether the computed solution actually satisfies them.
modules.why: Statics, circuits, numerical models, and estimation all lead to linear systems. Knowing how to question a solution matters as much as obtaining it.
explanation: A linear system A*x=b represents several coupled equations. Each row is an equation and each column corresponds to an unknown. Before typing matrices, write the unknown order explicitly and check coefficient units. A correct solver cannot repair a column that accidentally switched from one unknown to another halfway through the model. Begin with a two-equation system you can solve by substitution.

Use the backslash operator for a numerical solve rather than explicitly forming an inverse. Then calculate the residual A*x-b and inspect its size relative to the scale of the problem. A small residual means the computed answer satisfies the entered equations closely. It does not prove the equations represent reality, nor guarantee that the solution is insensitive to tiny changes in data.

Nearly dependent equations deserve attention. If two measurements provide almost the same information, small measurement differences can cause large changes in inferred unknowns. This is conditioning, not simply a MATLAB bug. Perturb one right-hand-side value slightly and observe the result. Later linear algebra courses explain norms, rank, and condition numbers; this module gives you concrete questions to carry into that mathematics.

example.explanation: The solution is [2;1], and the residual is zero up to numerical rounding.

walkthrough: Write both scalar equations and the unknown order.
Construct A and b with compatible dimensions.
Solve using backslash and substitute the result.
Change an input slightly and compare the solution change.
pitfalls: Using inv(A)*b as the default solve.
Calling a tiny residual proof that the physical model is correct.
Ignoring solver warnings about rank or near singularity.

exercises.title: Two equations
exercises.prompt: Solve 2x+y=5 and x-y=1, then substitute the result manually.
hints: Subtract or substitute on paper first.
The right-hand side is a column.
exercises.solution: A\b gives [2;1]; 2*2+1=5 and 2-1=1 verify both equations.
exercises.extension: Change the second right-hand side to zero and predict the result.

exercises.title: Residual audit
exercises.prompt: Check the proposed solution [1;1] against the same system.
hints: Subtract b in the stated direction.
exercises.solution: A*candidate=[3;0], so the residual is [-2;-1]. The candidate does not solve the entered equations.
tests: Reversing subtraction changes signs, not norm.
exercises.extension: Report per-equation residuals with the relevant units.

exercises.title: Sensitivity experiment
exercises.prompt: Compare solutions before and after changing the second entry of b by 0.0001.
hints: Subtract the two equations by hand.
exercises.solution: The difference equation has coefficient 0.0001 on the second unknown. A tiny data change therefore creates a large solution change.
tests: Both solutions can have small residuals.
A better-separated A should be less sensitive.
exercises.extension: Explain why more output digits would not fix uncertain inputs.

exercises.title: Unknown order mismatch
exercises.prompt: A model defines x=[forceA;forceB], but the second row’s coefficients were entered in reverse order. Can a small residual reveal the mistake?
exercises.inputs: Entered A differs from the intended equation.
exercises.expected: No: a solver can exactly solve the wrong system.
hints: Separate implementation verification from model validation.
exercises.solution: Audit the mapping from equations to columns and correct A. Recheck against an independently derived case, not only the residual.
tests: Every column keeps one unknown meaning.
exercises.extension: Add a diagram or variable-order table to the report.

review.question: What does the residual measure?
review.answer: How closely the computed values satisfy the equations that were actually entered.

review.question: Can a small residual coexist with a sensitive solution?
review.answer: Yes. An ill-conditioned system can be solved with a small residual while small input perturbations strongly change the answer.

modules.title: Integrating sampled power
modules.summary: Estimate accumulated energy from timestamped measurements and inspect sampling error.
modules.why: A rover or habitat consumes changing power. Multiplying one reading by total duration may miss the actual energy history.
explanation: An integral accumulates a rate over an interval. For power measured in watts and time in seconds, the area under the power curve is energy in joules. Sampled data does not reveal the complete curve, so numerical integration introduces an approximation. The trapezoidal rule assumes straight segments between neighboring samples and adds the resulting areas.

Pass actual timestamps to trapz. Calling trapz(power) alone assumes unit spacing, which is wrong when readings are ten seconds apart or irregularly spaced. Verify that time increases and that each power value belongs to the corresponding timestamp. Missing intervals deserve a stated policy; joining across a long gap makes a strong assumption about unobserved behavior.

Use a function with a known integral to evaluate your method before using real data. Constant and linearly changing power are especially useful because trapezoidal integration is exact apart from rounding. For a curved function, reduce the step size and compare results. This convergence experiment separates a coding error from an approximation that improves with better sampling. Calculus gives the interpretation; the program gives a reproducible numerical experiment.

example.explanation: The two trapezoids contribute 24 J and 51 J, totaling 75 J.

walkthrough: Draw the sample points and trapezoids.
Calculate each interval contribution by hand.
Use actual timestamps in trapz.
Compare a finer sampling of a known curved function.
pitfalls: Assuming one-second spacing without checking.
Integrating unsorted timestamps.
Treating interpolation across a data gap as a measurement.

exercises.title: Constant power
exercises.prompt: Integrate 5 W over four seconds from three samples.
exercises.solution: trapz(t,P)=20; independently 5 W*4 s=20 J.
exercises.extension: Try irregular times [0 1 4] with the same constant power.

exercises.title: Irregular trapezoids
exercises.prompt: Compute energy and each interval contribution.
exercises.solution: (10+14)/2*2=24; (14+20)/2*3=51. Their sum agrees with trapz.
tests: There are two intervals, not three.
exercises.extension: Plot cumulative energy at the sample times.

exercises.title: Convergence on a curve
exercises.prompt: Compare trapezoidal estimates of the integral of t^2 from 0 to 1 using steps 0.5 and 0.25.
hints: Generate the grid including both endpoints.
exercises.solution: The first error is 1/24; the second is 1/96. Here halving step divides the error by four. Do not generalize this ratio to arbitrary missing or noisy data.
exercises.extension: Try 0.125 and explain the pattern.

exercises.title: The missing time scale
exercises.prompt: A log sampled every 10 s is integrated using trapz(P). Explain the factor error.
exercises.solution: Use trapz(t,P) or trapz(P)*10 only when constant spacing is established.
tests: An irregular log must use its timestamp vector.
exercises.extension: Write a check rejecting nonincreasing time.

review.question: Why pass timestamps to trapz?
review.answer: They define the width and units of each interval, including irregular spacing.

review.question: What does convergence testing show?
review.answer: How a numerical result changes as resolution improves; it does not establish that the physical model is correct.

modules.title: Interpolation is an assumption
modules.summary: Align data carefully and distinguish interpolation from extrapolation.
modules.why: Sensors and simulations often report at different times. Comparing them requires an explicit rule for values between samples.
explanation: Interpolation estimates a value inside the range of supplied data. Linear interpolation connects adjacent observations by a straight segment. It is easy to explain and a useful starting point when no stronger model is justified. It is not a new measurement, and a denser interpolated curve does not contain more experimental information than the original samples.

Extrapolation asks for values outside the observed range and is a different risk. A sensor that warmed steadily for ten seconds need not continue at the same rate for an hour. Choose an explicit out-of-range policy: reject the query, retain a missing value, or use a separately justified model. Do not enable extrapolation simply to eliminate NaNs from a plot.

When comparing two logs, choose the comparison timestamps first and preserve the originals. Check time order, duplicate times, units, and gaps before interpolating. For a status flag or operating mode, a continuous interpolation may be meaningless; a previous-value rule could be appropriate only if the state is understood to persist. The engineering meaning of the quantity determines the mathematical operation.

example.explanation: The estimates are [25 32] °C. They lie halfway between adjacent samples.

walkthrough: Mark which query times lie inside the observed interval.
Calculate a midpoint by hand.
Interpolate with a named method.
Label estimated values separately from measured values.
pitfalls: Calling a dense interpolated curve higher-resolution evidence.
Extrapolating unintentionally.
Interpolating categorical state numbers as if they were physical magnitudes.

exercises.title: Midpoint estimate
exercises.prompt: Estimate temperature at 5 s with linear interpolation.
exercises.solution: interp1(t,T,5,"linear") gives 25. This follows the straight-line assumption.
exercises.extension: Estimate at 2 s and explain the weight.

exercises.title: Unequal interval
exercises.prompt: Estimate a value at 3 s using endpoints 1 s and 7 s.
hints: Apply that fraction to the value difference.
exercises.solution: 10+(2/6)*(22-10)=14. The timestamps are not array indices.
tests: The result lies between endpoint values.
exercises.extension: Implement the formula once and compare to interp1.

exercises.title: Overlap-only comparison
exercises.prompt: Find valid comparison times for two logs before interpolating.
exercises.inputs: A spans [0,20] s; B spans [5,25] s; query=[0 5 10 15 20 25]
exercises.solution: The shared interval is [max(0,5),min(20,25)]=[5,20]. Mask query times to this interval before computing differences.
exercises.extension: Report how much of each run is excluded.

exercises.title: A fractional operating mode
exercises.prompt: A mode log uses 0=idle and 1=active. Linear interpolation gives mode 0.5 between transitions. Diagnose it.
hints: Ask when the transition is known to occur.
exercises.solution: Do not apply continuous interpolation blindly. If a logged state persists until its next update, document and use previous-value behavior; otherwise mark the transition interval uncertain.
exercises.extension: Keep an uncertainty interval around unknown transition timing.

review.question: Does interpolation create new evidence?
review.answer: No. It creates estimates between supplied observations under a chosen rule.

review.question: What distinguishes extrapolation?
review.answer: The query lies outside the observed range, where the interpolation assumptions have no bracketing data support.

modules.title: Fit a model and question its residuals
modules.summary: Estimate a simple relationship while separating fitted values from validation evidence.
modules.why: Calibration and experiment analysis often need a model, but a high-order curve can hide problems rather than explain them.
explanation: Curve fitting chooses parameters that make a model agree with data according to an objective. For a first calibration exercise, fit a straight line and interpret its slope and intercept with units. A polynomial degree is a modeling choice, not a quality setting. More coefficients can reduce training residuals while making predictions unstable or physically implausible.

Residuals are measured values minus model predictions at the same inputs. Plot them against the input and against collection order. A trend may suggest missing physics, an offset may suggest calibration bias, and isolated outliers may suggest data problems. None of these patterns proves a cause by itself. Use them to decide which assumption or measurement deserves another experiment.

Keep some evidence separate from fitting when possible. A held-out observation tests prediction more honestly than a point used to select parameters. Also report the range over which data supports the fit; extrapolating a calibration line far beyond its observations can be unjustified. You need basic algebra for the line, while later statistics provides deeper tools for uncertainty and model comparison.

example.explanation: The fitted coefficients are approximately [2 1]. Residuals are zero up to rounding for this invented exact line.

walkthrough: Choose the model family before looking for a perfect curve.
Fit a line and interpret coefficient units.
Compute and plot residuals.
Test a held-out point and state the supported input range.
pitfalls: Choosing a high degree merely to pass through every observation.
Treating training fit as independent validation.
Reporting coefficients without units or input range.

exercises.title: An exact line
exercises.prompt: Fit a first-degree polynomial to four exact points and predict y at x=4.
hints: A line has slope and intercept.
MATLAB stores the highest-power coefficient first.
exercises.solution: polyfit(x,y,1) yields [2 1] within rounding; polyval(p,4)=9. This last point is extrapolated.
tests: All training residuals are near zero.
exercises.extension: Label the x=4 prediction as extrapolation.

exercises.title: Residual sign
exercises.prompt: Calculate residuals and identify whether predictions are high or low.
exercises.solution: Subtract corresponding values. A positive residual means the measured quantity exceeded the prediction under this convention.
exercises.extension: Make a labeled residual chart.

exercises.title: Hold out an observation
exercises.prompt: Fit the first three exact points, then evaluate a fourth observation without refitting.
hints: Do not include the test observation in polyfit.
Keep a separate variable for validation.
exercises.solution: The trained line is y=2x+1. At x=3 it predicts 7; the held-out observation differs by 0.4. Investigate whether that error is acceptable in context.
exercises.extension: Repeat with several held-out points.

exercises.title: Perfect but unhelpful
exercises.prompt: A student raises polynomial degree until every noisy calibration point is matched, then calls it validated. Explain the failure.
exercises.inputs: Six noisy samples and a degree-five polynomial.
exercises.expected: Interpolation of training samples does not establish predictive or physical validity.
exercises.solution: Use a justified simple model, inspect residuals, and evaluate separate data. Degree should reflect the question and data support, not a goal of zero training error.
tests: Check behavior between and outside observations.
exercises.extension: Compare line and quadratic using the same withheld data.

review.question: What does polyfit degree 1 represent?
review.answer: A straight-line least-squares model with slope and intercept.

review.question: Why inspect residuals?
review.answer: Their magnitude and structure expose disagreements hidden by an attractive overlaid curve and guide further validation.

modules.title: Solve an equation, then verify the root
modules.summary: Use a numerical root finder with a meaningful interval and an independent residual check.
modules.why: Engineering equilibrium and threshold questions often reduce to finding where a model equals a target.
explanation: A root is an input at which a function is zero. If you want a cooling model to reach 25 °C, subtract 25 from the model and solve the resulting equation. This reformulation is more useful than searching a plot by eye. Define the physical domain and units before calling a solver, and inspect the function near the proposed interval.

A bracket with opposite endpoint signs is useful for a continuous function because it identifies a crossing. It does not guarantee that every function is appropriate for the method: discontinuities, invalid model regions, and roots that only touch zero require care. fzero returns a numerical answer together with diagnostics that should be read rather than ignored.

After solving, evaluate the original model at the returned input and check the residual in meaningful units. Ask whether the root lies within the model’s supported domain and whether multiple roots could answer different questions. For a simple exercise, compare against algebra. This creates a habit of treating numerical solvers as tools for a specified problem instead of mysterious buttons that confer correctness.

example.explanation: The positive root is 3. The bracket selects the positive crossing rather than the negative root.

walkthrough: Rearrange the target condition into f(x)=0.
Inspect endpoint values and continuity assumptions.
Call the solver with a justified interval.
Substitute the answer into the original condition.
pitfalls: Solving in a physically invalid domain.
Ignoring diagnostics or a large residual.
Assuming the returned root is the only possible root.

exercises.title: A known root
exercises.prompt: Find the positive root of x^2-9 using [0,5].
exercises.solution: fzero(@(x)x.^2-9,[0 5]) returns approximately 3; 3^2-9=0.
tests: The result is within the bracket.
exercises.extension: Find the negative root with a different bracket.

exercises.title: A threshold time
exercises.prompt: Solve when T(t)=20+20*exp(-t/30) reaches 25 °C.
hints: Use algebra as a second method.
exercises.solution: 20*exp(-t/30)=5 gives t=30*log(4). The numeric solver should agree within tolerance.
exercises.extension: Change target to 30 °C and compare times.

exercises.title: No finite crossing
exercises.prompt: Explain why the same model never reaches exactly 20 °C at a finite nonnegative time.
hints: The exponential remains positive for finite t.
Separate a tolerance threshold from exact equality.
exercises.solution: Do not force a finite root by extending the interval. Define a practical condition such as T-20<=0.1 if that is scientifically justified.
tests: T(t)>20 for finite t in exact arithmetic.
A tolerance target above 20 has a finite crossing.
exercises.extension: Solve the 0.1 °C difference threshold analytically.

exercises.title: A sign change at a jump
exercises.prompt: A piecewise function is -1 below x=0 and +1 at or above x=0. Does a sign-changing bracket prove it has a root?
exercises.expected: No; the function never equals zero.
hints: Evaluate the function at the proposed answer.
exercises.solution: The intermediate-value argument does not apply across a jump. A solver’s location near zero is not a valid zero-residual solution.
exercises.extension: Construct a continuous comparison function.

review.question: Why evaluate the residual after solving?
review.answer: It verifies that the returned input actually satisfies the intended numerical condition.

review.question: Why does a bracket need context?
review.answer: Sign changes can come from discontinuities or invalid model regions, and the physical domain may exclude some mathematical roots.

modules.title: Differential equations and a cooling model
modules.summary: Simulate a first-order system and compare the numerical trajectory to a known solution.
modules.why: Dynamics and thermal engineering describe rates of change. Coding makes those equations testable, provided the physical assumptions stay visible.
explanation: This lesson belongs after introductory calculus and differential equations. The model dT/dt=-(T-Ta)/tau says the temperature changes in proportion to its difference from a fixed ambient temperature. A positive time constant creates passive relaxation. This is a lumped model: the entire object has one temperature, with constant parameters and no spatial gradients.

An ODE solver needs the rate function, a time interval, and an initial condition. It returns a numerical trajectory, not the physical truth. Begin with this equation because its analytic solution is available. Compare numerical and analytic values at the same returned times; comparing mismatched grids can create an artificial error. Tightening solver tolerances is a numerical experiment, not a way to repair a wrong physical equation.

Before adding another state, verify initial value, direction, units, and limiting behavior. If the object starts warmer than ambient, it should cool toward ambient without overshooting in this model. If it starts at ambient, it should remain there. Real systems can violate these predictions because of internal heat generation, varying airflow, radiation, multiple thermal masses, or sensor lag. Those are reasons to revise the model after evidence, not to hide the disagreement.

example.explanation: The analytic comparison uses the solver’s returned time vector. The rate has units °C/s when tau is in seconds.

walkthrough: Derive the rate units and state the assumptions.
Evaluate the derivative at the initial condition.
Integrate and compare with the analytic solution.
Test equal initial and ambient temperatures.
pitfalls: Missing the minus sign.
Comparing solutions at different timestamps.
Calling a one-temperature model a detailed thermal analysis.

exercises.title: Initial derivative
exercises.prompt: Calculate the initial cooling rate before running a solver.
hints: Positive temperature difference should produce cooling.
exercises.solution: -(40-20)/30=-0.666666... °C/s. A positive result would reveal a sign mistake.
tests: At T=Ta the derivative is zero.
At T below Ta the derivative is positive.
exercises.extension: Explain why a temperature difference can be expressed in K or °C.

exercises.title: One time constant
exercises.prompt: Compare numerical and analytic temperature at t=30 s.
hints: The remaining temperature difference is multiplied by exp(-1).
Request or evaluate the solution at the same time.
exercises.solution: Use the analytic expression as the reference. The system has removed about 63.2% of its initial difference after one time constant.
exercises.extension: Repeat at two time constants.

exercises.title: Tolerance study
exercises.prompt: Run the model with two solver tolerance settings and compare maximum analytic error on each returned grid.
exercises.inputs: Use RelTol 1e-3 then 1e-6 with a suitable AbsTol.
exercises.expected: Both should approximate the analytic curve; report measured errors rather than inventing fixed values.
hints: Use odeset and read its documentation.
Compare at each run’s own t values.
exercises.solution: Calculate max(abs(T-exact(t))) separately. Numerical errors depend on solver settings and implementation; record actual results and function evaluations if investigated.
tests: Neither result is called experimentally validated.
exercises.extension: Repeat for a longer time interval.

exercises.title: Heating by mistake
exercises.prompt: The implemented derivative is +(T-Ta)/tau for a warmer-than-ambient object. Diagnose the growing trajectory.
exercises.expected: The sign is wrong for passive cooling.
hints: A solver faithfully integrates the supplied equation.
exercises.solution: Use the negative sign derived from heat flowing toward ambient. Changing plotting limits or tolerances does not fix the physics.
exercises.extension: Write a monotonicity test that catches the sign error.

review.question: What information does an ODE solver require?
review.answer: A derivative function, initial condition, time interval, and optional numerical controls such as tolerances.

review.question: What is a lumped thermal assumption?
review.answer: The modeled object is represented by one uniform temperature instead of a spatial temperature field.

modules.title: Sampling, spectra, and honest frequency claims
modules.summary: Inspect a simple periodic signal without confusing FFT output with unlimited frequency knowledge.
modules.why: Vibration and rotating machinery produce time series. Sampling choices limit what those series can reveal.
explanation: Begin after learning basic trigonometry and the idea of frequency. A sampled signal records values at discrete times. Its sampling rate determines which frequencies can be distinguished without ambiguity under the sampling assumptions. A fast oscillation can masquerade as a slower one when undersampled; no colorful spectrum can recover information that was never recorded.

The FFT efficiently computes a discrete Fourier transform. To interpret its output, you must know the sample spacing, sample count, scaling convention, and whether you are looking at a one-sided or two-sided spectrum. Start with a noise-free sinusoid whose frequency falls exactly on a DFT bin. That removes several complications and gives you a known reference for the frequency axis.

Real logs introduce trends, finite-record effects, noise, nonuniform timestamps, and multiple components. Windowing and detrending are useful later topics, but they should not be applied as unexplained rituals. Do not pass irregularly timed samples to a uniform-sampling FFT and label the result in hertz without addressing the timing. Base MATLAB provides fft; other signal-processing functions may require a licensed toolbox, so check each function’s product requirements.

example.explanation: This is a two-sided magnitude display with peaks at 5 Hz and its mirrored bin at 95 Hz. It is not yet a one-sided amplitude plot.

walkthrough: Define sample rate, count, and duration convention explicitly.
Generate a known bin-centered sinusoid.
Build the frequency axis from Fs/N.
Explain mirrored bins before interpreting a real log.
pitfalls: Labeling array index as hertz.
Treating irregular samples as uniformly spaced.
Confusing two-sided magnitude scaling with one-sided amplitude.

exercises.title: Sample times
exercises.prompt: Create 100 samples at 100 Hz beginning at zero. State the final timestamp.
hints: A sample count is not a final index.
exercises.solution: t=(0:N-1)/Fs. There are 100 samples, separated by 0.01 s.
exercises.extension: Contrast sample span with a one-second periodic record convention.

exercises.title: Frequency bins
exercises.prompt: Compute the DFT bin spacing and identify bins for a 5 Hz sinusoid.
exercises.expected: Spacing 1 Hz; zero-based bins 5 and 95. MATLAB indices 6 and 96.
exercises.solution: The positive component is at f=5; the conjugate mirror is at f=95 in the full DFT array.
tests: A DC signal peaks at MATLAB index 1.
The frequency vector has N elements.
exercises.extension: Create a correctly scaled one-sided plot after reading the fft example.

exercises.title: Aliasing thought experiment
exercises.prompt: At a 100 Hz sample rate, compare sampled cosines at 10 Hz and 90 Hz at integer sample times.
exercises.expected: They produce the same ideal samples.
exercises.solution: At integer n, cos(2*pi*n-2*pi*10*n/100)=cos(2*pi*10*n/100). The samples alone cannot distinguish these cases.
tests: Maximum difference is near rounding error.
Changing the sampling rate can break the ambiguity.
exercises.extension: Describe why an analog antialias filter may be needed.

exercises.title: Index masquerading as frequency
exercises.prompt: A spectrum is plotted with plot(abs(fft(x))) and its x-axis labeled Hz. Diagnose what is missing.
exercises.expected: Bin spacing is 2 Hz, not 1 Hz.
exercises.solution: Use f=(0:N-1)*Fs/N and specify the scaling convention. Otherwise peak labels are numerically wrong and shifted by the indexing origin.
exercises.extension: Add a caption naming the spectrum convention.

review.question: What fixes the DFT bin spacing?
review.answer: The ratio Fs/N for uniformly sampled data.

review.question: Does a longer FFT created by zero padding add measured information?
review.answer: No. It samples the transform representation more densely without adding new observations.

modules.title: Parameter sweeps and uncertainty experiments
modules.summary: Vary assumptions systematically and keep random experiments reproducible.
modules.why: A single simulation run can conceal sensitivity. Exploring plausible inputs helps you see which assumptions deserve better measurements.
explanation: A parameter sweep evaluates the same model over a deliberate set of inputs. Change one parameter first so the resulting pattern is easy to understand. Store both input and output for every run; a plot of unlabeled results is not a reproducible experiment. Choose ranges from the question and available evidence, not from what produces the most dramatic figure.

Uncertainty experiments go a step further by sampling from stated distributions. A random number generator makes computational samples, but it does not justify the distribution. Uniform, normal, independent, and correlated assumptions have different meanings. Begin with a simple repeatable random sequence and record the algorithm and seed. Reproducibility lets you compare code changes without confusing them with a changed random draw.

Distinguish sensitivity from probability. A worst-case parameter grid is not automatically a confidence interval, and a Monte Carlo percentile is conditional on the assumed input model. Report what was varied, what was held fixed, and what was not modeled. Base MATLAB supports simple random sampling; specialized statistics features can have separate product requirements. For early work, a transparent range study is often more valuable than an elaborate unjustified probability claim.

example.explanation: The deterministic sweep gives about [20.9957,22.7067,24.4626] °C. The seed is relevant when random sampling is added.

walkthrough: Define the question and plausible parameter range.
Run one-at-a-time variations before combinations.
Store inputs beside outputs.
If sampling randomly, record seed, generator, distribution, and limitations.
pitfalls: Calling a sweep a statistical confidence interval.
Changing the random sample while comparing two implementations.
Assuming independent inputs without examining the physical relationship.

exercises.title: Three time constants
exercises.prompt: Calculate temperature at 60 s for three time constants.
exercises.solution: The remaining difference is 20*exp(-60/tau). The sequence increases because larger tau retains more of the initial warmth.
exercises.extension: Plot output against tau with units.

exercises.title: Repeatable random draws
exercises.prompt: Generate five uniform random numbers twice by resetting the same named generator and seed.
exercises.expected: The two generated vectors agree exactly in the same environment.
hints: Do not reset between individual values in one vector.
exercises.solution: Save first=rand(1,5), reset the generator and seed, then second=rand(1,5). Compare with isequal.
tests: An additional draw advances the sequence.
exercises.extension: Record MATLAB release alongside generator metadata.

exercises.title: A bounded input model
exercises.prompt: Sample a time constant uniformly between 20 and 40 s and propagate it through the cooling formula. Explain the limitation.
exercises.expected: All sampled tau lie in [20,40); temperatures lie within the corresponding deterministic bounds.
hints: The distribution is an assumption, not a measurement.
exercises.solution: Compute each output and summarize sample statistics. Interpret any percentile only under the uniform time-constant assumption.
exercises.extension: Compare the result with a different justified distribution.

exercises.title: A seed inside the loop
exercises.prompt: A simulation resets rng(7) before every iteration, then draws one random input. Why are all trials identical?
exercises.expected: Each iteration restarts the same sequence.
hints: Distinct draws require advancing generator state.
exercises.solution: Set the seed once before sampling. The repeated experiment is then reproducible while individual trials can differ.
tests: At least two draws differ under normal operation.
Rerunning the entire experiment reproduces all draws.
exercises.extension: Explain why identical trials invalidate an intended Monte Carlo sample.

review.question: What does a random seed establish?
review.answer: A reproducible computational sequence under the specified generator and environment, not the truth of an uncertainty model.

review.question: How does sensitivity differ from uncertainty?
review.answer: Sensitivity asks how outputs respond to changed inputs; uncertainty analysis also models what is known or assumed about those inputs.

modules.title: A reproducible engineering report
modules.summary: Package inputs, calculations, checks, and limitations into an analysis another person can rerun.
modules.why: A portfolio project earns credibility through traceable evidence, not only a polished figure.
explanation: A useful report connects a question to data, a model, a result, and a limitation. Separate raw inputs, analysis functions, tests, and generated outputs. Use explicit filenames and relative project paths rather than a private absolute path tied to one computer. Store units and variable definitions beside the data so someone opening the project later can interpret it without asking you.

Exporting a table is an interface decision. Specify column names, numeric meaning, missing-data representation, and whether a repeated run replaces or creates a new output. For a learning project, write into a dedicated output directory and preserve the original observations. Reimport one exported result and compare its row count and key values; this catches formatting and schema mistakes at the boundary.

End with an honest statement of scope. A cooling notebook can demonstrate numerical modeling without proving a habitat thermal design. A frequency plot can reveal a component without identifying its mechanical cause. Include one failed hypothesis or limitation you investigated. As your classes deepen the physics, return to the same project and improve one assumption at a time. This makes the report a growing body of evidence instead of a finished screenshot.

example.explanation: Run in a dedicated scratch/output folder. The file is a generated result, not the original measurement record.

walkthrough: Write a README with the question, setup, and run order.
Keep raw input separate from generated output.
Export labeled results and verify a round trip.
Add model assumptions, a known test, and a limitation.
pitfalls: Publishing a figure without the input and code needed to regenerate it.
Overwriting raw data with cleaned results.
Presenting a classroom model as certified design evidence.

exercises.title: Labeled result table
exercises.prompt: Create and export a three-row table with units in column names.
exercises.expected: A CSV with named columns and three data rows.
hints: Write to a scratch output folder.
exercises.solution: table(time_s,voltage_v) retains meaningful variable names. Reimport the exported CSV and inspect its columns.
exercises.extension: Add a run identifier column.

exercises.title: One-command rerun
exercises.prompt: Design a run_all.m script that validates inputs, calls a model, runs checks, and exports results in a documented order.
exercises.expected: A fresh session recreates the same report outputs.
hints: Fail before exporting if validation fails.
exercises.solution: The driver owns workflow; functions own calculations. Include explicit input paths and a final output summary.
tests: A missing input produces a clear diagnostic.
Two runs with the same inputs agree.
exercises.extension: Record runtime and MATLAB release in metadata.

exercises.title: Cross-language handoff
exercises.prompt: Specify a CSV contract for Python to read a MATLAB-generated thermal trajectory.
exercises.inputs: Columns time_s,temperature_c; one row per sample.
exercises.expected: Both languages agree on row count, units, order, and missing-value policy.
hints: CSV alone does not explain units.
Write a short schema beside it.
exercises.solution: Document UTF-8 text, comma delimiter, header names, seconds from start, °C values, increasing times, and how missing values are represented.
tests: Compare a known value within an explicit tolerance.
exercises.extension: Build a Python verification script in a later project.

exercises.title: A report that cannot be rerun
exercises.prompt: A report contains only a final plot and a script referring to an unnamed variable loaded manually. Identify the minimum repair.
exercises.inputs: No input file or run instructions included.
exercises.expected: Provide input or a reproducible synthetic substitute, explicit loading, units, and run order.
hints: Ask what a fresh computer lacks.
Distinguish private data from shareable sample data.
exercises.solution: Make the dependency explicit and include a small public fixture that exercises the same analysis path. State any omitted data limitation.
tests: The fixture runs without manual workspace setup.
exercises.extension: Add a verification checklist to the README.

review.question: What is the smallest credible analysis package?
review.answer: A clear question, interpretable input or fixture, runnable code, a known check, reproducible outputs, and stated limitations.

review.question: Why round-trip an exported table?
review.answer: It tests the file interface that another tool or future user will actually consume.

modules.title: Build C deliberately, not accidentally as C++
modules.summary: Create a hosted C program and understand the compiler contract.
modules.why: C helps you understand firmware interfaces and machine constraints. Learning it as a separate language avoids misleading assumptions from C++.
explanation: C and C++ share much syntax but are distinct languages with different rules and idioms. Start with a .c file, a C compiler driver, and an explicitly selected language standard. For GCC or Clang, a useful desktop learning command is cc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic main.c -o sample. Other toolchains use different flags, so record the actual tool and command you used.

A hosted C program usually begins at main and can use the standard library available in that environment. A microcontroller project may be freestanding, with startup code, linking rules, and libraries supplied by its toolchain and board support package. Do not treat a desktop program and a board binary as interchangeable simply because both contain C source. Begin on the desktop where tests and diagnostics are easy to inspect.

Use one tiny calculation to make every build step observable. Write source, compile it, inspect diagnostics, run the exact executable you built, and compare with a predicted output. Distinguish a language error from a link failure and a wrong calculation. The first lasting habit is preserving enough evidence that you can reproduce the same result after your tools or directory layout change.

example.explanation: The program prints 1.500 s. Floating-point division is paired with a matching printf format.

walkthrough: Save the example as a .c file.
Select C17 explicitly in a supported toolchain.
Resolve the first diagnostic before later ones.
Record expected output and the exact executable path.
pitfalls: A C++ driver can accept or reject code under different rules.
A desktop library may not exist on a microcontroller.
Running an old executable after a failed build can hide the failure.

exercises.title: First reproducible result
exercises.prompt: Change the duration to 2750 ms and rebuild.
