exercises.solution: Divide before printing and verify three digits after the decimal point.
exercises.extension: Write a one-command build instruction.

exercises.title: Identify the failure stage
exercises.prompt: Create separate examples of a missing semicolon and a declared but undefined function.
exercises.solution: The compiler needs valid syntax; the linker needs an implementation for each called function.
tests: Confirm no old executable is mistaken for the new version.
exercises.extension: Repeat from your editor and command line.

exercises.title: Desktop versus board
exercises.prompt: Compare startup and output assumptions in this sample with a board project.
exercises.inputs: Desktop standard output; board UART unconfigured
exercises.expected: A table of assumptions rather than a claimed drop-in port
exercises.solution: Desktop runtime and output are provided by the environment; embedded startup and I/O redirection depend on the selected platform.
exercises.extension: Plan a fake I/O interface.

exercises.title: Wrong language mode
exercises.prompt: A C file is compiled with g++ and gives confusing diagnostics. Fix the build first.
exercises.expected: Use a C compiler mode and C17 selection
hints: Extension alone may not override the driver.
exercises.solution: Use cc, gcc, or clang in C mode with -std=c17 where supported, or document an equivalent toolchain setting.
tests: Confirm the build log shows the intended command.
exercises.extension: Explain why Arduino sketches are typically C++.

review.question: Why select a language standard?
review.answer: It makes the accepted language contract explicit instead of relying on changing defaults.

review.question: What does hosted mean?
review.answer: An environment providing normal C startup and library facilities, unlike many bare-metal projects.

modules.title: Integer ranges, units, and conversion order
modules.summary: Choose representation intentionally and test limits before ordinary data.
modules.why: Embedded measurements often begin as integer counts; scaling needs both a sensor model and correct arithmetic.
explanation: A number has a representation before it has a physical meaning. An ADC count may be stored in an unsigned integer, while the voltage estimate is a floating-point calculation based on a documented reference and range. A learning model might map integer counts 0 through 4095 onto 0 through 3.3 volts. That is a model to test, not a substitute for a particular converter's datasheet.

Integer arithmetic happens before assignment to a floating-point destination when both operands are integers. Multiplication can overflow before a later conversion appears to fix it. Decide where to convert and what intermediate range is required. Unsigned arithmetic follows modular rules; signed overflow is undefined behavior. Neither should be used accidentally to handle an out-of-range physical measurement.

limits.h describes properties of ordinary integer types, and stdint.h provides fixed-width types when supported. uint16_t does not promise that every arithmetic expression uses sixteen bits: integer promotions still apply. Begin with explicit input-range checks and simple double scaling. Study fixed-point arithmetic when the project gives you a reason, and preserve an independently calculated reference result for comparison.

example.explanation: A simulated 12-bit endpoint model with a 3.3 V reference; invalid counts or a null output pointer are rejected.

walkthrough: State raw range and physical units.
Predict endpoints and midpoint.
Convert before fractional arithmetic.
Verify invalid input leaves output unchanged.
pitfalls: ADC transfer models depend on the device.
Casting after truncation or overflow is too late.
Fixed-width storage does not eliminate promotions.

exercises.title: Endpoint scaling
exercises.prompt: Evaluate the conversion at both endpoints.
hints: Compare floats with a justified tolerance.
exercises.solution: Zero produces zero; maximum count produces a ratio of one.
exercises.extension: Calculate 2048 counts and explain its relation to 1.65 V.

exercises.title: Reject without mutation
exercises.prompt: Initialize output to 9 and call with invalid counts.
exercises.solution: The guard returns before writing the caller-owned result.
tests: Valid zero changes output to zero.
exercises.extension: Document every error path.

exercises.title: Fixed-point range analysis
exercises.prompt: Analyze multiplication before converting counts to integer millivolts.
exercises.solution: A uint32_t intermediate can represent the product where available; divide by 4095 and explicitly choose truncation or rounding.
exercises.extension: Compare integer and double models for every raw count.

exercises.title: Nearly every result is zero
exercises.prompt: Repair double ratio = counts / 4095 before scaling.
exercises.solution: Use counts / 4095.0. Assigning an integer-division result to double cannot recover its fractional part.
exercises.extension: Retain a midpoint regression test.

review.question: Does signed overflow wrap predictably?
review.answer: No. It is undefined behavior; use checked arithmetic.

review.question: Why test endpoints?
review.answer: They provide easy independent checks of range, units, and arithmetic order.

sources.title: GNU C language introduction and reference (includes GNU extensions)

modules.title: Functions and output-pointer contracts
modules.summary: Use explicit return status and caller-owned outputs.
modules.why: C interfaces often communicate through pointers; meaning, validity, and lifetime must be clear.
explanation: C passes function arguments by value. Passing a pointer copies an address value, allowing the function to access an object owned by the caller. This often returns a calculation result while the function's return value reports success or failure. The interface should say whether the pointer may be null, which object is modified, and what happens to that object when the operation fails.

A pointer is not a length, ownership record, or proof of validity. A non-null pointer can refer to an object whose lifetime ended or to inappropriate storage. A scalar output parameter requires a pointer to a live object of the correct type. Arrays also require a count. The caller and function share responsibility for honoring this contract; checking only null cannot establish arbitrary pointer safety.

Keep the implementation auditable: validate what you can before modifying caller-visible output. Compute into local variables and assign on success. This gives a simple failure guarantee and makes tests clearer. Avoid global variables as hidden outputs; their values and ordering dependencies complicate isolated tests and later concurrency. Draw the caller object and the copied pointer to understand which object each assignment affects.

example.explanation: The output must point to a live double. This avoids forming a+b first, though rounding and non-finite policy still matter.

walkthrough: Write validity and ownership requirements.
Return status independently from value.
Test success and null rejection.
Document non-finite input behavior.
pitfalls: Non-null does not prove validity.
Changing the local pointer does not change the caller's pointer.
Partial output changes on failure complicate callers.

exercises.title: Caller-owned result
exercises.prompt: Call mean_pair with the address of a local result.
exercises.solution: The copied pointer permits writing into the caller's live double.
exercises.extension: Reject non-finite input.

exercises.title: No mutation on failure
exercises.prompt: Design a conversion that rejects negative duration and preserves output.
exercises.solution: Return failure for negative duration before writing; keep computation local until all validation succeeds.
exercises.extension: Use distinct status codes for different errors.

exercises.title: Two results without globals
exercises.prompt: Return minimum and maximum for two finite inputs using a small result struct.
exercises.solution: A struct keeps results coherent; a status field or checked output pointer communicates validity.
tests: Swapped inputs give the same result.
Equal inputs give equal min and max.
exercises.extension: Extend to an array and count.

exercises.title: Address of a dead local
exercises.prompt: Repair a function returning the address of its automatic local result.
exercises.expected: Return double by value or write through a caller output pointer
hints: Copying an address does not extend lifetime.
exercises.solution: Returning the scalar is simplest; if status is needed, accept an output pointer supplied by the caller.
exercises.extension: Draw lifetimes for both repaired interfaces.

review.question: Are pointer arguments passed by reference in C?
review.answer: No. The pointer value is copied; dereferencing it may access a caller-owned object.

review.question: What is a useful failure guarantee?
review.answer: Caller-visible output remains unchanged unless the operation succeeds.

modules.title: Arrays, sizes, and bounds-aware interfaces
modules.summary: Carry the number of accessible elements beside every buffer.
modules.why: Parser and sensor code becomes easier to reason about when each access is tied to a known bound.
explanation: An array is a contiguous sequence of elements, but a pointer to its first element does not carry its count. In most expressions an array converts to such a pointer. A function parameter written double values[] is adjusted to a pointer parameter; sizeof(values) there measures the pointer, not the original array. Pass the element count explicitly and distinguish it from a byte count.

If n is the number of accessible elements, valid indexes run from zero through n-1. Stop loops before n and define empty-input behavior. Do not read the first element before checking that one exists. A pointer-plus-count contract must also say whether null with zero count is allowed. Choose a consistent rule, then test all combinations of empty and nonempty inputs.

Bounds checks work only when the caller supplies an honest count for live storage. C cannot recover the true allocation size from an arbitrary pointer. Keep ownership local, derive counts from real arrays when possible, and pass sizes through layers without inventing them. For external packets, verify length before reading fields even when every normal example happens to be long enough.

example.explanation: The caller promises n accessible doubles. Empty input is accepted with sum zero, including NULL when n is zero.

walkthrough: Draw indexes and the one-past-end position.
Pass size_t count with the pointer.
Test zero, one, and several elements.
Check that validation precedes each access.
pitfalls: i <= n reads one element too many.
sizeof an array parameter does not recover caller length.
An exaggerated count is invalid even with a non-null pointer.

exercises.title: Sum a bounded array
exercises.prompt: Call sum_values on the supplied sequence.
exercises.solution: Visit indexes 0,1,2 only.
exercises.extension: Write a mean that rejects empty input.

exercises.title: Null-and-empty policy
exercises.prompt: Test buffer and count combinations with a valid output pointer.
hints: No access is needed for zero count.
exercises.solution: NULL is rejected only when n>0; zero-count input yields an empty sum.
exercises.extension: Compare with a stricter always-non-null contract.

exercises.title: Bounded maximum
exercises.prompt: Implement maximum without an empty-input sentinel.
hints: Initialize from element 0 only after n>0.
Zero is wrong for all-negative data.
exercises.solution: Check nonempty, initialize from the first element, and scan the rest with i<n.
exercises.extension: Define non-finite behavior.

exercises.title: One-past-end loop
exercises.prompt: Repair a loop with condition i<=n.
exercises.solution: Use i<n and preserve a zero-length regression test.
exercises.extension: Explain why an apparently harmless adjacent read is still invalid.

review.question: What information does a pointer omit?
review.answer: Accessible length, ownership, and lifetime guarantees.

review.question: Why use size_t for counts?
review.answer: It is the standard unsigned type for object sizes and sizeof results, though arithmetic still needs care.

modules.title: Strings are buffers with an ending convention
modules.summary: Keep capacity, length, and termination separate.
modules.why: Readable telemetry labels still occupy finite memory; a copied name must not overwrite the next object.
explanation: A C string is a sequence of character values terminated by a null character. Its logical length excludes that terminator, but storage must include space for it. A char array is not automatically a valid string: without a terminator inside accessible storage, string operations may keep reading beyond the object. Know whether an interface accepts a string or an arbitrary sequence of bytes.

Capacity describes available storage; length describes text currently present. Before copying, establish whether text plus terminator fits. Define the overflow policy: reject, truncate with a visible status, or allocate more storage. Silently truncating a sensor identifier can merge two sources into one displayed name, creating a data-integrity bug even when memory writes remain inside the destination.

Prefer interfaces receiving destination capacity and returning a result you check. snprintf supports bounded formatting, but its result is the number of characters that would have been written, excluding the terminator. A nonnegative result at least as large as capacity indicates truncation. Check before treating the output as complete. Practice exact-fit and one-too-small cases before embedding formatted text in a larger parser.

example.explanation: Reports whether the complete label fits. On truncation the destination can contain a shortened string; this is not an unchanged-on-failure interface.

walkthrough: Count visible characters plus one terminator.
Document capacity and overflow behavior.
Test exact fit and one byte too small.
Check formatting status before using an identifier.
pitfalls: strlen requires a valid terminated string.
strncpy can leave output unterminated.
Bounded truncation can still corrupt meaning.

exercises.title: Exact label capacity
exercises.prompt: Find minimum storage for two labels.
exercises.solution: Three characters need four bytes; five need six.
tests: Capacity 3 cannot hold all of S42.
exercises.extension: Recalculate after adding a prefix.

exercises.title: Detect truncation
exercises.prompt: Format id 1234 into capacity 4.
exercises.expected: false; shortened output is not a complete identifier
exercises.solution: The label needs six bytes. The return check detects truncation despite bounded writing.
exercises.extension: Return a distinct Truncated status.

exercises.title: Unchanged on failure
exercises.prompt: Design a copy function that rejects insufficient space without modifying output.
exercises.solution: Validate length against capacity before copying. An explicit source length avoids relying on an unbounded scan.
exercises.extension: Use source pointer plus length.

exercises.title: Unterminated name
exercises.prompt: A three-byte array contains R,O,V and is printed with %s. Repair it.
exercises.inputs: Three characters without a null terminator
exercises.expected: Use a four-byte terminated string or length-aware output
exercises.solution: Declare char name[]="ROV" to include the terminator, or use an explicitly bounded byte-output operation.
exercises.extension: Explain text versus binary packet bytes.

review.question: Is every char array a string?
review.answer: No. A terminator must exist within accessible storage.

review.question: What does snprintf result >= capacity mean?
review.answer: The full formatted output did not fit.

modules.title: Structs, enums, and explicit validity
modules.summary: Group measurements with the state needed to interpret them.
modules.why: Valid zero, stale data, and missing observations deserve different representations.
explanation: A struct groups related fields into one record. An enum names a finite set of states. Together they represent value, time, and quality without hiding missing data in a magic number. Function interfaces become easier to read and tests can construct the condition they intend to exercise. Initialize every field that later code may read, including status fields that seem obvious.

Struct assignment copies member values, but a pointer member still refers to the same external object after copying. It does not clone the pointed-to buffer or transfer ownership automatically. Prefer scalar fields and small fixed arrays for early sensor records. Introduce pointer fields when their ownership, lifetime, and access permissions are explicit, especially if records outlive the function that built them.

An in-memory struct is not automatically a portable wire format. A compiler may add padding; alignment, integer sizes, and byte order can vary. Writing sizeof(struct sample) bytes directly to a file therefore does not establish a reliable interchange format. Keep the logical record separate from the byte encoding, define field widths and order, and test encoding against fixed known fixtures.

example.explanation: The time type is illustrative; its range and clock meaning must be defined by the real interface.

walkthrough: Define validity states.
Initialize every field.
Test one record per state.
Keep encoding separate from record layout.
pitfalls: Pointer members copy shallowly.
Uninitialized data is not a missing-data detector.
Raw struct bytes include representation assumptions.

exercises.title: Zero can be real
exercises.prompt: Classify records by quality.
exercises.solution: Quality preserves the distinction independently of the number.
tests: Valid negative temperature remains usable in this narrow contract.
exercises.extension: Add domain validation separately.

exercises.title: Copy semantics
exercises.prompt: Copy a record with one scalar and one buffer pointer; describe what changes.
exercises.inputs: Two structs point to one buffer
exercises.expected: Scalar values copy; buffer remains shared
hints: Draw two records and one buffer.
exercises.solution: Editing one scalar does not change the other record; editing the common buffer is visible through both pointers.
exercises.extension: Compare with a fixed array embedded in the struct.

exercises.title: Encode the contract
exercises.prompt: Write a separate byte-format table for a centidegree reading and a quality byte.
exercises.expected: Offsets, widths, signedness, and order stated
hints: Do not use sizeof(struct) as format.
exercises.solution: A decoder can validate a known packet length and reconstruct logical fields without assuming compiler layout.
exercises.extension: Add a format-version field.

exercises.title: Padding surprise
exercises.prompt: Raw struct files differ across compilers. Repair the design.
exercises.solution: Define external bytes deliberately and decode them independently of in-memory layout.
tests: Two encoders emit the same fixture.
exercises.extension: Explain why packing alone is not a full portability solution.

review.question: Does struct copy clone a pointed-to buffer?
review.answer: No. It copies the pointer value.

review.question: Why separate record and encoding?
review.answer: Logical meaning should not depend on compiler layout or host byte order.

modules.title: Bit masks and byte order without guesswork
modules.summary: Decode flags and multi-byte fields explicitly.
modules.why: Telemetry decoders should explain every bit and every byte they read.
explanation: A mask selects positions in an integer. If bit zero means stale, (status & 1u) != 0 tests that bit independently of other flags. Use unsigned types and named masks. Logical && asks whether whole expressions are true, while bitwise & combines corresponding bits. Confusing them can pass a simple test and fail as soon as a different flag is set.

Byte order describes a multi-byte representation. For a big-endian two-byte unsigned field, the first byte is the high part: first*256 + second. Decode explicitly instead of casting a byte pointer to a wider integer pointer. A cast can introduce alignment, aliasing, and host-byte-order assumptions while concealing the format's actual meaning. The external contract chooses the byte order.

Bounds still come first. Correct arithmetic cannot rescue reading a second byte from a one-byte input. Validate pointer and length, construct the result in an unsigned type wide enough for intermediate operations, then assign. The examples assume fixed-width types are available. Real interfaces should verify these platform assumptions and distinguish unknown reserved bits from currently recognized flags.

example.explanation: Reads an unsigned big-endian value without assuming host byte order or alignment.

walkthrough: Create a named bit-position table.
Test flags alone and combined.
Decode one fixture by hand.
Reject short input before access.
pitfalls: Logical and bitwise AND are different.
Widen before shifting.
A wider pointer cast is not a portable decoder.

exercises.title: Independent flags
exercises.prompt: Decode stale at bit 0 and fault at bit 2.
exercises.solution: Status 5 is binary 0101 and contains both named flags.
exercises.extension: Report unknown reserved bits.

exercises.title: Endian fixture
exercises.prompt: Decode two bytes in both orders.
exercises.extension: Write an inverse encoder.

exercises.title: Reserved bit policy
exercises.prompt: Only bits 0 and 2 are allowed. Reject others.
exercises.solution: For an eight-bit status, status & 0xFAu identifies reserved bits.
exercises.extension: Version the policy for future flags.

exercises.title: Logical-AND decoder
exercises.prompt: Code uses status && 4u for bit 2. Find a failing case.
exercises.solution: Replace with (status & 4u) != 0u; && ignores bit positions.
exercises.extension: Exhaustively test all 256 statuses.

review.question: Why widen before shifting?
review.answer: It makes intermediate signedness and range explicit.

review.question: Who decides byte order?
review.answer: The external format contract, not the host machine.

modules.title: Parse numbers while retaining error information
modules.summary: Distinguish zero from malformed or out-of-range text.
modules.why: Weak configuration parsing can turn a typo into a plausible parameter.
explanation: Text conversion must answer more than what number appeared first. Determine whether any digits were consumed, whether the whole expected token was consumed, and whether the value fits the accepted range. strtol provides an end pointer and range-error reporting that support those checks. A wrapper should preserve their information instead of treating every failure as numeric zero.

Choose a grammar. A strict field may permit decimal digits only, while a more permissive field permits leading whitespace and an optional sign. strtol accepts syntax your application might forbid, so library success is not automatically grammar success. Select base ten when decimal is the contract, then validate any additional restrictions explicitly and explain them in the error message.

Reset errno immediately before conversion, inspect conversion progress and the end pointer, check ERANGE, and then enforce application limits before narrowing. Validate before changing caller-visible output. Test zero, empty text, a number followed by junk, a huge number, and exact boundaries. A bad-then-good two-call test catches dependence on error state left behind by an earlier operation.

example.explanation: Accepts strtol leading whitespace and optional sign, requires full consumption, and limits the result to 0..1000. Stricter grammar needs additional checks.

walkthrough: Write the token grammar.
Check progress and full consumption.
Check range before narrowing.
Verify output remains unchanged on rejection.
pitfalls: atoi lacks the same end-pointer interface.
A numeric prefix is not a complete token.
errno is not automatically cleared on success.

exercises.title: Successful zero
exercises.prompt: Test zero, empty text, and letters.
exercises.solution: Only the zero token produces an in-range completed conversion.
exercises.extension: Decide whether +0 is allowed.

exercises.title: Numeric prefix
exercises.prompt: Test full-token consumption.
exercises.solution: The library can parse a prefix, but the wrapper requires no remaining character.
exercises.extension: Create a separate unit-suffix parser.

exercises.title: Strict decimal grammar
exercises.prompt: Allow digits only, no signs or whitespace.
exercises.solution: Reject empty text or any nondigit, then perform checked conversion and apply 0..1000 limits.
exercises.extension: Return separate syntax and range statuses.

exercises.title: Stale errno
exercises.prompt: A valid conversion fails because errno still contains ERANGE.
exercises.inputs: Valid 10 after a failed prior call
hints: Tie error state to one call.
exercises.solution: Set errno=0 immediately before strtol and retain end-pointer and range checks.
tests: Bad then good succeeds on second call.
exercises.extension: Add a two-call regression test.

review.question: What does end tell you?
review.answer: Where conversion stopped and whether no characters were consumed.

review.question: Why check before narrowing?
review.answer: A long result may exceed the application or destination range.

modules.title: Storage duration, lifetime, and borrowed pointers
modules.summary: Draw which objects exist and who may still access them.
modules.why: A pointer value can survive long after its object is gone; explicit lifetime reasoning prevents subtle defects.
explanation: Storage duration determines how long an object is available. An ordinary local variable usually has automatic storage duration and ceases to exist when execution leaves its block. A static object lasts for the program's execution. Dynamically allocated storage lasts until it is released. Scope, which controls where a name can be used, is related but not identical to lifetime.

A pointer can borrow access without owning the object. If a function receives a pointer to caller data, the caller normally remains responsible for keeping that data alive and eventually releasing it if appropriate. Document whether the function retains the pointer after returning. A function that stores a borrowed address for later use has a stronger lifetime requirement than one that reads it immediately.

Draw a timeline for each object and every pointer that refers to it. A non-null pointer is not proof that its target still exists, and setting one pointer to null does not invalidate other aliases automatically. Static storage can avoid one dangling-pointer bug while introducing hidden shared state and reentrancy problems. Choose lifetime based on the interface, not as a shortcut around understanding ownership.

example.explanation: The view borrows storage and does not extend its lifetime. The zero fallback is an explicit demonstration policy, not an appropriate missing-data policy for every application.

walkthrough: Draw automatic, static, and allocated object lifetimes.
Mark pointers as owners or borrowers in notes.
State whether functions retain pointers.
Test APIs with caller-owned data that stays alive for the whole use.
pitfalls: Returning a pointer to an automatic local creates a dangling pointer.
A static local can create shared mutable state.
Null checks do not detect expired or otherwise invalid addresses.

exercises.title: Borrowed view
exercises.prompt: Pass a view of a live three-element array and inspect its first value.
hints: The view copies pointer and count.
exercises.solution: The function reads element zero while the caller's array is alive.
tests: A null zero-count view performs no read.
exercises.extension: Replace fallback with explicit status.

exercises.title: Retention contract
exercises.prompt: Compare a function that immediately sums a buffer with one that stores its pointer for tomorrow's callback.
exercises.expected: The retaining function requires a longer lifetime
hints: Ask when the last read occurs.
Returning does not necessarily end access.
exercises.solution: Document the retention interval or copy the data into owned storage. Immediate use only requires validity during the call.
tests: Caller cannot destroy retained data early.
A copied buffer has a separate lifetime.
exercises.extension: Design an API that makes retention obvious.

exercises.title: Remove static scratch state
exercises.prompt: A parser returns a pointer to a static result reused on every call. Redesign it for two independent results.
hints: Static avoids local expiration but is shared.
Accept output pointers or return structs.
exercises.solution: Store each parsed result in a distinct caller object and stop sharing hidden scratch output.
tests: Second parse does not alter first result.
exercises.extension: Explain reentrancy separately from thread safety.

exercises.title: Two aliases, one release
exercises.prompt: After free(a), code sets a=NULL but still reads alias b that pointed to the same allocation. Diagnose it.
exercises.inputs: a and b referred to one allocation
exercises.expected: b is dangling and must not be read
hints: Nulling a does not update b.
exercises.solution: Release invalidates access through all aliases; redesign ownership so borrowers end before release.
tests: The ownership diagram names one releaser.
exercises.extension: Use a sanitizer to detect an isolated test defect where supported.

review.question: Is scope the same as lifetime?
review.answer: No. Scope governs name visibility; lifetime governs whether the object exists.

review.question: Does a borrowed pointer extend lifetime?
review.answer: No. The owner must keep the object alive for every permitted use.

modules.title: Allocation, capacity, and one clear owner
modules.summary: Allocate only after checking size arithmetic and define who releases memory.
modules.why: Dynamic memory can be useful, but its failure and ownership paths are part of the design.
explanation: malloc requests a number of bytes and can fail. Before multiplying an element count by an element size, prove that the multiplication fits size_t. Otherwise an overflow can request a much smaller allocation than intended while later code still assumes the original large count. Keep requested count and actual capacity together, and reject unreasonable application sizes before allocating even when arithmetic would fit.

C does not automatically release allocations when a pointer leaves scope. Name the one owner responsible for free and document whether a function transfers ownership or merely borrows access. Every successful allocation should have a visible release path, including errors after allocation. Prefer a bounded fixed array when the maximum size is small and truly known; dynamic allocation is not a requirement for sophisticated software.

realloc has special failure behavior: on failure, the original allocation remains valid. Assigning its return value directly to the only owning pointer can therefore lose the original address. Use a temporary pointer and replace the owner only after success. Define a zero-size policy explicitly rather than relying on implementation-sensitive expectations. This module is for desktop experiments; embedded projects may impose stricter allocation rules.

example.explanation: Returns either an owned allocation for n doubles or NULL. The caller must initialize elements before reading and release the allocation exactly once.

walkthrough: Check count against a realistic application limit.
Check multiplication before allocation.
Handle NULL before access.
Identify the single owner and every release path.
pitfalls: Allocated bytes are not automatically initialized by malloc.
Losing the only pointer leaks the allocation.
Double-free and use-after-free are invalid regardless of whether a run crashes.

exercises.title: Byte requirement
exercises.prompt: Compute storage for 100 doubles using the actual implementation size.
hints: Do not assume a size without checking.
The count is elements, not bytes.
exercises.solution: Use sizeof *pointer or sizeof(double) and check multiplication before requesting bytes.
exercises.extension: Print both count and byte capacity.

exercises.title: Failure injection
exercises.prompt: Wrap allocation so a test can force failure and verify the caller.
exercises.expected: No write or read through NULL; explicit failure result
hints: Do not wait for real memory exhaustion.
exercises.solution: Inject a controlled allocator result and ensure no output claims a successfully created buffer.
tests: Failure path frees nothing it never acquired.
exercises.extension: Count live allocations in the test wrapper.

exercises.title: Resize without losing ownership
exercises.prompt: Write the control flow for growing an allocation using a temporary realloc result.
exercises.inputs: Existing owned buffer; simulated failed growth
exercises.expected: Original owner remains valid on failure
hints: Do not overwrite the owner yet.
exercises.solution: tmp=realloc(owner,new_bytes); if tmp is non-null update owner and capacity, otherwise keep both old values.
exercises.extension: Document that newly added bytes need initialization.

exercises.title: Overflow before malloc
exercises.prompt: A function requests n*sizeof(double) without checking and then loops n times. Repair the size path.
hints: Allocation success cannot validate an overflowed request.
exercises.solution: Test n > SIZE_MAX/sizeof(double) before multiplying, and also apply a practical maximum count.
exercises.extension: Test with a fake allocator to avoid huge real allocations.

review.question: Who frees an owned result?
review.answer: The caller if the API transfers ownership, as stated explicitly in the contract.

review.question: Why use a temporary realloc result?
review.answer: Failure leaves the original allocation valid; overwriting its only address would lose it.

modules.title: Files, exact byte counts, and portable records
modules.summary: Read and write small binary fixtures without confusing partial data with complete records.
modules.why: Sensor logs and telemetry packets need explicit lengths and representation rules.
explanation: A file operation can return fewer elements than requested. A short read may mean end-of-file or an error, so the caller must examine both the count and the stream state before deciding what happened. For a fixed-size record, receiving only part of the record is not successful decoding. Keep I/O separate from the decoder so the same byte fixture can test parsing without touching a file.

Define the external record byte by byte: a version, flags, and a two-byte reading can make a useful four-byte educational format. State byte order and units, and reject unknown versions or forbidden flags. This discipline is more important than a fancy checksum. A checksum can detect certain accidental changes but does not fix an ambiguous format or establish authenticity.

Opening, reading, writing, and closing all have outcomes worth checking. Close streams on every owned path, preserve the original input, and avoid presenting a partial output as a completed report. A beginner-friendly workflow writes to a new file and validates it by reading it back with an independent fixture expectation. Never assume raw struct bytes form a portable external format.

example.explanation: The caller provides four writable bytes. A false result can leave partial bytes written; inspect feof/ferror in the I/O layer if that distinction is needed.

walkthrough: Define one fixed-size external format.
Test decoder directly with byte arrays.
Check exact fread/fwrite counts.
Test truncated files and retain failure reasons.
pitfalls: Array syntax in a parameter does not enforce destination capacity.
Short reads may partially modify a buffer.
A checksum is neither a format definition nor an authenticity guarantee.

exercises.prompt: Define version=1, flags=0, reading=258 in big-endian form.
exercises.solution: Version and flags occupy the first two bytes; 258 is 0x0102 in the final pair.
exercises.extension: Create a second fixture with maximum reading.

exercises.prompt: Attempt to read a fixed four-byte record from files of length 0,1,3,4.
exercises.expected: Only length 4 is a complete record
exercises.solution: Gate decoding on an exact four-byte read. Report an incomplete record or I/O error through the surrounding interface.
exercises.extension: Distinguish clean empty file from partial final record.

exercises.prompt: Read three four-byte records and detect an incomplete tail.

exercises.solution: Process exact groups of four; when the final read returns two, report an incomplete record at offset 12.

exercises.extension: Write a text summary without altering input.

exercises.prompt: Code treats any nonzero fread return as one complete four-byte record. Fix it.

exercises.solution: Require a count of four before decoding. Preserve the distinction between partial read and valid record.
exercises.extension: Explain how changing size/count arguments changes the return-count unit.

review.question: Can a failed fixed-record read modify output?
review.answer: Yes. Partial bytes may already have been written.

review.question: Why separate I/O and decoding?
review.answer: The decoder can be tested with deterministic byte arrays, and I/O errors remain distinguishable.

modules.title: Warnings, sanitizers, and boundary-driven testing
modules.summary: Build a small test harness that reports failures in every build configuration.
modules.why: C demands deliberate checks around memory and arithmetic; a clean happy-path run is weak evidence.
explanation: Start from the interface contract and make a boundary table. A two-byte decoder needs tests for lengths zero, one, two, and extra bytes under its policy. A range-limited number parser needs below-minimum, minimum, maximum, above-maximum, and malformed input. Give each case a name explaining the promised behavior. A failed test should tell you what assumption was violated, not only that something went wrong.

Compiler warnings expose many suspicious constructs before execution, but their coverage depends on the toolchain and settings. A debugger reveals actual values and control flow. On supported platforms, AddressSanitizer detects categories of memory misuse and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer detects selected undefined operations on executed paths. They complement careful reasoning and tests; none is a certificate that every possible input is safe.

Make the harness itself trustworthy. assert may disappear when NDEBUG is defined, so durable test verdicts should use explicit checks or a test framework. Have at least one deliberate known-failing case during harness development to confirm it exits nonzero. Keep failing inputs as regression fixtures, and use a fake allocator or fake clock for failures that should not depend on exhausting memory or waiting real time.

example.explanation: This minimal harness reports failure independently of assert settings. Replace the trivial arithmetic check with real interface cases.

walkthrough: Build a contract boundary table.
Verify the harness detects a deliberate defect.
Run normal and diagnostic builds.
Keep the smallest reproducing fixture after every fix.
pitfalls: An unexecuted branch is not covered by a sanitizer run.
Warnings cannot validate units or intended physics.
Disabled assertions can make an empty test run appear successful.

exercises.title: Decoder length table
exercises.prompt: List outcomes for a decoder requiring at least two bytes.
hints: Extra bytes need a deliberate rule.
exercises.solution: The guard n<2 rejects the first two cases; successful parsing reads only the first pair.
exercises.extension: Compare an exact-length policy.

exercises.title: Validate the test runner
exercises.prompt: Temporarily change a correct expected value to a wrong one.
exercises.expected: Nonzero process exit and named diagnostic
exercises.solution: Explicit failure accounting should make automation detect the failed case regardless of release assertions.
exercises.extension: Register the harness with CTest.

exercises.title: Exhaust a small input space
exercises.prompt: Test an eight-bit flag decoder for every possible status.
hints: Expected bit2 follows integer division by 4 modulo 2.
exercises.solution: Compare each decoder result to an independently expressed arithmetic oracle, not a copied implementation.
exercises.extension: Check reserved-bit rejection exhaustively.

exercises.title: The silent release tests
exercises.prompt: A release build compiles away all assert checks. Repair evidence collection.
exercises.expected: Explicit runtime checks still detect wrong output
hints: Do not equate zero exit with executed assertions.
exercises.solution: Use a real test runner or explicit comparisons and failure counts; retain a harness self-check during development.
tests: Run debug and release test builds.
Inject then remove a known defect.
exercises.extension: Record test case counts.

review.question: What is a regression fixture?
review.answer: An input preserving a previously observed defect so the fix stays checked.

review.question: Can warnings and sanitizers replace contracts?
review.answer: No. They detect selected implementation issues, not intended behavior or physical validity.

modules.title: Finite-state machines as plain C data and functions
modules.summary: Model a simulated device workflow with explicit events and transitions.
modules.why: C can express reliable state logic without a large object hierarchy or hidden mutable flags.
explanation: A finite-state machine represents a small set of modes and the events that change them. Use an enum for states, another enum for events, and a function that computes the next state. Begin with a transition table on paper. It should cover normal progress, irrelevant events, reset, and the loss of expected data. Two independent booleans often accidentally represent impossible combinations that one state enum excludes.

Keep transition decisions separate from physical actions. A pure transition function can be tested on the desktop and replayed from a fixture. Another layer carries out a requested action, records its outcome, and supplies a later event if needed. This separation prevents a half-completed I/O operation from being mistaken for a successful state change and makes unexpected failures easier to represent.

Every default behavior is still a policy. Ignoring an event, reporting an error, or moving to Review can each be sensible under different requirements. State the choice and test it. The educational example models environmental logging only; real embedded equipment needs domain-specific analysis, recovery design, and hardware validation beyond the correctness of one transition function.

example.explanation: Unlisted state/event combinations retain the current state. Invalid numeric enum values still require an external-input validation policy.

walkthrough: Write a complete state/event table.
Separate action requests from decisions.
Replay normal and bad-sample sequences.
Test reset from every state.
pitfalls: An enum does not validate arbitrary incoming integers by itself.
Default behavior must be intentional.
Multiple independent mode flags can represent impossible states.

exercises.title: Normal logging sequence
exercises.prompt: Replay START,SAMPLE_OK,FINISH from IDLE.
hints: Apply one event at a time.
exercises.solution: Only START and FINISH cause transitions in this sequence.
exercises.extension: Record an event-by-event trace.

exercises.title: Bad sample sequence
exercises.prompt: Replay START,SAMPLE_BAD,FINISH.
hints: FINISH is only accepted in SAMPLING.
exercises.solution: After SAMPLE_BAD the machine remains in REVIEW until a defined recovery event, currently RESET.
exercises.extension: Add a documented review-completed event.

exercises.title: Full transition tests
exercises.prompt: Create table-driven tests for every valid state and event.
exercises.solution: Each table entry specifies expected next state; reset should lead to IDLE from all four states.
tests: No state/event pair is left implicit in the test table.
exercises.extension: Return a separate accepted/ignored event result.

exercises.title: Illegal numeric event
exercises.prompt: A byte from a file is cast to enum event without range validation. Repair the boundary.
hints: Enum storage does not prove semantic validity.
exercises.solution: Map only defined byte codes to known enum values, returning an explicit unknown-event error for others.
exercises.extension: Keep the raw byte in a diagnostic record.

review.question: Why use a pure transition function?
review.answer: It enables deterministic replay and complete table tests without hardware.

review.question: Does enum type eliminate all invalid values?
review.answer: No. Values from casts or external representations still need semantic validation.

modules.title: Ring buffers, bounded capacity, and timer rollover
modules.summary: Make a small queue whose invariants remain visible at empty, full, and wrap boundaries.
modules.why: Embedded software often needs bounded storage and predictable overload behavior.
explanation: A ring buffer reuses a fixed array by moving indexes around its capacity. The data does not need to shift every time an item leaves. A simple beginner design keeps a head index and an explicit count. The next write position is (head+count) modulo capacity, while removal advances head and decreases count. State the invariants: head is inside the array and count never exceeds capacity.

Full and empty are different states even when some indexes coincide. A count makes that distinction explicit, at the cost of maintaining one more value consistently. Choose what a full buffer does: reject a new item, overwrite the oldest, or ask a producer to wait. The example rejects new items and reports failure. It is single-threaded; sharing it between threads or interrupts requires additional platform-appropriate synchronization.

Timer counters can also wrap. Unsigned subtraction can represent elapsed ticks across one wrap when the true interval remains within the counter's modulus and the surrounding assumptions are satisfied. Do not generalize this into comparing arbitrary absolute timestamps with ordinary less-than. For this module, test wraparound with a deliberately tiny simulated counter so the cases are visible without waiting for real hardware.

example.explanation: Initialize as struct ring q={0}. This bounded single-threaded push rejects a full or invalid queue; a matching pop must preserve the same invariants.

walkthrough: Write capacity, head, and count invariants.
Test empty, exact-full, and rejected push.
Add pop and verify wraparound order.
Keep concurrency outside this first implementation.
pitfalls: Index coincidence alone can confuse empty and full.
Overwriting old data must be an explicit policy.
Unsigned elapsed-time tricks require stated range and wrap assumptions.

exercises.title: Fill and reject
exercises.prompt: Push five values into an empty capacity-four ring.
exercises.expected: First four succeed; fifth fails; count stays 4
hints: Failed push must not mutate the queue.
exercises.solution: The fifth value is rejected under this policy, preserving the four earlier values.
tests: Rejected push does not change head.
exercises.extension: Return a distinct Full result.

exercises.title: Wrap while preserving order
exercises.prompt: Fill with 1,2,3,4; pop two; push 5,6; then pop all.
exercises.solution: The reused slots hold newer values while head still identifies the oldest retained item.
exercises.extension: Log internal indexes after every operation.

exercises.title: Tiny timer rollover
exercises.prompt: Compute elapsed ticks with an eight-bit modulo model.
exercises.inputs: Previous 250; current 5; fewer than 256 true elapsed ticks
exercises.solution: There are six increments from 250 to 0 and five more to 5. The answer is only unambiguous under the stated interval bound.
tests: 250 to 250 gives zero under no-full-wrap assumption.
exercises.extension: Explain why two full wraps cannot be detected from endpoints alone.

exercises.title: Shared queue illusion
exercises.prompt: An interrupt and main loop modify head and count without synchronization. Can volatile fix the queue invariant?
exercises.expected: No; use a platform-appropriate concurrency design
exercises.solution: Design interrupt-safe ownership or critical sections using the actual platform contract; retain the single-threaded version as a reference model.
tests: Document which context writes each field.
Test policy independently of hardware timing.
exercises.extension: Study an appropriate single-producer/single-consumer design later.

review.question: Why keep count in a beginner ring buffer?
review.answer: It makes full and empty explicit while providing an invariant to test.

review.question: Does volatile make compound queue updates atomic?
review.answer: No. Synchronization and atomicity require separate reasoning and platform facilities.

modules.title: Hardware boundaries, volatile, and fake devices
modules.summary: Keep portable logic separate from device-specific access.
modules.why: A clean boundary lets you test the program before a disconnected wire or board setup hides a logic error.
explanation: A hardware adapter translates device-specific operations into an interface your program can reason about. It might provide a read operation returning status plus a raw value, while portable code validates and scales the result. Keep register addresses, bus calls, and board initialization inside that adapter. A desktop fake can implement the same interface with a planned sequence of successful and failed reads.

volatile tells the compiler that certain accesses have special observable meaning; it does not make a compound operation atomic, establish inter-thread synchronization, or validate a register sequence. Real hardware requires the device datasheet, processor memory model, toolchain guidance, and board support APIs. Do not copy a register address from an unrelated board and expect the language to make it correct.

Use dependency injection in its simplest C form: pass a function pointer and an opaque context pointer to the component that needs input. The fake context can hold sample data and an index. Test ordinary readings, disconnection, stale values, and recovery without physical hardware. Once portable behavior is clear, integrate one real operation at a time and compare its observed contract with the fake assumptions.

example.explanation: The adapter owns the meaning of context and output-on-failure. This fragment performs no hardware access and can be tested with a fake reader.

walkthrough: Define the read interface and failure policy.
Implement a deterministic fake context.
Test disconnect and recovery sequences.
Consult actual device documentation before a hardware adapter.
pitfalls: Volatile is not a concurrency primitive.
A fake is useful only if its contract matches the intended device boundary.
Register layout and timing are platform-specific.

exercises.title: Constant fake device
exercises.prompt: Implement a fake reader that always returns 1234 successfully.
hints: The fake need not use context.
exercises.solution: Assign the predetermined count and return success, making the calling logic testable on the desktop.
tests: Null function pointer is rejected by take_sample.
exercises.extension: Convert the fake count using the validated ADC model.

exercises.title: Disconnect sequence
exercises.prompt: Create a fake returning success, failure, success.
exercises.expected: Two valid samples and one explicit missing observation
hints: Failure is not a zero reading.
Do not silently reuse the previous value as fresh.
exercises.solution: Advance the fake sequence and preserve status. The consumer records missing data for the middle call.
exercises.extension: Add timestamps to distinguish stale from missing.

exercises.title: Context-backed replay
exercises.prompt: Store a fixture array and index in a fake context; reject reads beyond its end.
hints: Cast context only inside its documented adapter.
exercises.solution: The context owns replay position. Each successful read advances once; exhaustion returns failure without out-of-bounds access.
exercises.extension: Add injected errors at selected indexes.

exercises.title: Volatile as a lock
exercises.prompt: A comment says volatile unsigned count makes ++count safe across interrupts and threads. Correct it.
exercises.expected: Volatile does not guarantee atomic read-modify-write or synchronization
hints: An increment involves multiple logical steps.
exercises.solution: Use the platform's documented atomic or critical-section mechanism and define the concurrency model rather than relying on volatile.
tests: Portable logic has no unnecessary shared state.
exercises.extension: Explain the separate role volatile can have for memory-mapped I/O.

review.question: Why use a fake device?
review.answer: It makes data and failure sequences deterministic so portable behavior can be tested first.

review.question: What does a function pointer plus context provide?
review.answer: A small interface for substituting different implementations while carrying implementation-specific state.

modules.title: A reusable C component and a reviewable portfolio
modules.summary: Package a bounded component with a header, implementation, tests, and explicit guarantees.
modules.why: Understanding a small trustworthy component is a better foundation than importing a flight framework you cannot explain.
explanation: A component needs a clear public interface and a small set of responsibilities. Place declarations, documented types, and caller obligations in a header. Keep private helper functions and state inside the implementation where possible. A header should be usable from a clean source file without depending on accidental include order. Build a small test executable against the same implementation used by the demonstration.

Write a compact trace from each requirement to evidence. A packet decoder might require rejection of short data, recognition of a version byte, and preservation of output on failure. Map those to named tests and fixed byte fixtures. Include compiler settings and the intended C standard. This record helps future you understand whether a change preserved the original contract or intentionally replaced it.

Mature flight-software ecosystems such as NASA cFS demonstrate how reusable services, applications, and platform abstractions fit together. Read them for architecture after you can explain your own component. Framework use, C language choice, and passing tests do not confer flight qualification. A credible project report distinguishes tested behavior, assumptions, portability limits, and future verification work without diminishing what the prototype actually achieved.

example.explanation: A public interface sketch. The implementation must document null-pointer policy, expected length, allowed flags, and output behavior before it can be considered complete.

walkthrough: Write the interface contract and include guard.
Keep implementation helpers private.
Map each requirement to a test.
Rebuild from clean source and publish a limitations note.
pitfalls: A header declaration is not an implemented or verified contract.
A framework does not transfer qualification to your project.
Platform assumptions should be stated rather than disguised as portability.

exercises.title: Requirement trace
exercises.prompt: Turn reject invalid packets into three specific testable requirements.
exercises.expected: Three named requirements and corresponding tests
exercises.solution: Require minimum length, recognized version, and unchanged output on rejection; give each one a fixed fixture.
exercises.extension: Add reserved-flag behavior.

exercises.title: Standalone header check
exercises.prompt: Compile a source file that includes only the public header before its main function.
exercises.expected: Header compiles using its own declared dependencies
hints: The header must include size_t and integer declarations.
exercises.solution: Include stddef.h and stdint.h in the header because its public types require them.
exercises.extension: Add C++ linkage guards only if interoperability is required.

exercises.title: cFS architecture reading
exercises.prompt: Read the official cFS repository overview and map application, platform abstraction, and tests to your own component.
exercises.expected: A sourced one-page comparison with explicit unknowns
exercises.solution: Describe the shared separation-of-concerns idea while clearly identifying the much smaller scope and unverified aspects of the learning component.
tests: Every framework claim links to its source.
exercises.extension: Follow one official sample application later.

exercises.title: Overclaimed reliability
exercises.prompt: A README calls a desktop parser flight-safe because it uses C and passes 20 tests. Rewrite it.
exercises.solution: State tested inputs, compiler, diagnostic tools, and known limits; list hardware, timing, and domain assurance as unperformed work.
exercises.extension: Prioritize the next test by a realistic failure mode.

review.question: What belongs in a public header?
review.answer: Types, declarations, dependencies, and clear caller obligations needed to use the interface.

review.question: What makes a prototype report credible?
review.answer: Reproducible evidence, explicit assumptions, and honest limits alongside its demonstrated capabilities.

modules.title: Know which shell you are using
modules.summary: Orient yourself before running commands and create a disposable learning workspace.
modules.why: Robotics instructions often assume Linux and Bash. Recognizing the environment prevents confusing a shell problem with a programming problem.
explanation: Bash is a command interpreter and scripting language. Linux is an operating-system kernel used in many complete environments. A terminal is the window or interface through which you interact with a shell. PowerShell is a different shell with different syntax and object-based behavior. A command copied from one environment may not mean the same thing in another, even if a familiar command name exists.

On Windows, an installed WSL distribution is one possible place to use Linux tools; Git Bash is another environment with different capabilities. Neither should be assumed to contain every robotics dependency. Identify the shell, current directory, and available command before following a tutorial. Read-only checks such as pwd, printf, and command -v help establish where you are without changing system settings.

Practice in a fresh scratch directory, not among irreplaceable project files. The example creates a unique temporary directory and enters it, so repeated lessons do not overwrite earlier work. Write down the path it prints. This is not a cleanup lesson: leave deletion to a deliberate later action after inspecting the contents. Your first success is knowing exactly where a command runs and which files it can affect.

example.code:
printf "Bash version: %s\n" "$BASH_VERSION"
pwd
lab_dir=$(mktemp -d) || exit 1
cd "$lab_dir" || exit 1
printf "Practice directory: %s\n" "$PWD"
example.explanation: Run these commands in Bash. mktemp creates a unique directory, and quoted cd preserves its path as one argument.

walkthrough: Identify whether the active shell is Bash or PowerShell.
In Bash, inspect the version and current directory.
Create and enter a new temporary directory.
Write the directory path in your learning notes.
pitfalls: Assuming the terminal application determines the shell language.
Pasting Bash assignments into PowerShell.
Running file exercises in an important project directory.

exercises.title: Environment inventory
exercises.prompt: In Bash, print its version and current directory. Explain what each tells you.
exercises.expected: A Bash version string and an absolute current-directory path.
hints: pwd reports location, not shell identity.
exercises.solution: printf "%s\n" "$BASH_VERSION"; pwd. The version identifies Bash behavior; the path identifies the base for relative filenames.
tests: Version is not empty in Bash.
pwd agrees with the directory you intended.
exercises.extension: Record the operating environment separately.

exercises.title: Command discovery
exercises.prompt: Determine whether python3 and git are available without executing a project.
exercises.expected: Paths or a nonzero status if a command is absent.
hints: command -v asks how a command resolves.
Absence is information, not permission to install blindly.
exercises.solution: Inspect each command separately and record which environment supplied it. An installed Windows program and a Linux command may differ.
tests: A deliberately invented command does not.
exercises.extension: Compare with your project’s documented prerequisites.

exercises.title: Workspace map
exercises.prompt: Create a new temporary directory and draw a plan for raw, work, and results subdirectories.
exercises.expected: All proposed paths stay under the printed practice directory.
hints: Use mkdir with relative names after entering the directory.
exercises.solution: Create the three subdirectories with mkdir raw work results. Use pwd and a listing to confirm location before adding sample files.
exercises.extension: Describe which category should contain unmodified observations.

exercises.title: Wrong-shell diagnosis
exercises.prompt: A tutorial says sample_count=3, but the current console interprets it as a command. Identify the likely cause before changing syntax.
exercises.inputs: A PowerShell console running Bash tutorial text.
exercises.expected: The user must choose Bash or translate intentionally to PowerShell.
hints: A terminal window can host different shells.
exercises.solution: The assignment syntax belongs to Bash. Follow the tutorial in a supported Bash environment or use equivalent PowerShell instructions consistently.
tests: BASH_VERSION is available in the intended Bash session.
The chosen tutorial matches the environment.
exercises.extension: Explain why Linux installation is separate from learning one assignment.

review.question: What is the difference between a terminal and a shell?
review.answer: The terminal provides the interaction surface; the shell interprets commands and implements a language.

review.question: Why start in a scratch directory?
review.answer: It bounds file effects and makes the lesson’s inputs and outputs easy to inspect.

modules.title: Paths and arguments with spaces
modules.summary: Treat a filename as data and preserve it as one command argument.
modules.why: Engineering folders often contain spaces, run names, and long descriptive filenames. Quoting is a daily reliability skill.
explanation: A command receives a list of arguments, not the exact sentence you see on screen. Bash first interprets quoting and expansions, then constructs that list. Unquoted spaces separate words. Quotes let a path such as run one remain one argument rather than becoming two unrelated names. This is why quoting is more than a style preference.

Single quotes preserve literal text. Double quotes allow selected expansions, such as a variable’s value, while keeping that result together. Use double quotes around a path variable in ordinary commands. The quote characters are instructions to the shell and are not normally part of the filename received by the command. To understand a command, ask how many arguments it will receive and what each contains.

Relative paths are resolved from the current working directory. A leading ./ makes that relationship explicit, and it also helps distinguish a filename beginning with a dash from an option. Many tools support -- to end option parsing, but verify the tool’s interface rather than assuming every program does. Practice with printf before copying or processing files so you can see the intended argument boundaries.

example.code:
run_name="run one"
mkdir -- "$run_name"
printf "<%s>\n" "$run_name" "./$run_name"
example.explanation: The two printf arguments remain intact. This example assumes a fresh practice directory where run one does not already exist.

walkthrough: Predict how many arguments a command receives.
Compare literal single quotes and expanding double quotes.
Create a directory with a space in its name.
Inspect the resulting path with a visible delimiter format.
pitfalls: Leaving path variables unquoted.
Including quote characters inside a variable as if they will become shell syntax later.
Confusing a relative path with a fixed absolute location.

exercises.title: One name, one argument
exercises.prompt: Print the name rover log between angle brackets without splitting it.
exercises.solution: printf "<%s>\n" "$name" preserves the value as one argument.
tests: A value containing two spaces remains intact.
exercises.extension: Try a value containing an asterisk without expanding filenames.

exercises.title: Literal versus expanded
exercises.prompt: Predict the difference between printing a literal variable reference and its value.
exercises.expected: Single quotes around $name print $name; double quotes print sensor A.
hints: Double quotes preserve boundaries while allowing variables.
exercises.solution: Use printf "%s\n" followed by each quoted form and compare. The quotes themselves are not printed.
tests: The literal form starts with a dollar sign.
The expanded form remains one argument.
exercises.extension: Explain which form suits a fixed template.

exercises.title: A filename beginning with dash
exercises.prompt: Design a read-only command to inspect a file named -notes.txt in the current scratch directory.
exercises.expected: The name is interpreted as a file, not an option.
exercises.solution: cat -- "./-notes.txt" makes both the option boundary and relative location explicit. Check cat’s help if using a nonstandard implementation.
tests: The path stays in the current directory.
exercises.extension: Explain how a variable containing that name should be quoted.

exercises.title: Quotes stored in a string
exercises.prompt: A variable contains the characters double-quote, run one, double-quote. A command still splits it when expanded unquoted. Why?
exercises.expected: Quote the expansion; do not store shell syntax as data.
hints: Expansion results are not reparsed as fresh quoting syntax.
Keep the variable’s value equal to the actual path.
exercises.solution: Set path="run one", then use "$path". Do not use eval to force reparsing.
tests: The variable contains no extra quote characters.
printf with delimiters shows one intact argument.
exercises.extension: Describe why reparsing strings as commands is fragile.

review.question: Why quote a path variable?
review.answer: To preserve its value as one argument and avoid unintended word splitting or filename expansion.

review.question: Do quotation marks inside a variable become shell quoting?
review.answer: No. They are data after expansion, not a second pass of shell syntax.

modules.title: Variables, defaults, and integer arithmetic
modules.summary: Use small pieces of state without turning the shell into a numerical analysis language.
modules.why: A run script needs filenames, counters, and modes. Scientific arrays and floating-point calculations usually belong in Python or MATLAB.
explanation: Bash assignments have no spaces around the equals sign. A variable can hold a string, including text that looks numeric. Expansion retrieves that string, and quoting preserves it. Use descriptive names such as run_label or sample_count. Avoid overwriting environment variables whose established meaning controls how tools behave.

Default values can make a script convenient, but a default should not conceal a missing essential input. For an optional label, a documented fallback is reasonable. For an input dataset, an absent path should usually produce a clear error. Distinguish an unset value from an empty one when that difference matters, and keep the behavior in the script’s usage text.

Bash arithmetic is integer arithmetic. Division truncates toward an integer result, so it is inappropriate for a scientific average such as 5/2 when you expect 2.5. Use the shell to coordinate a numerical program instead of recreating its data model. Be cautious with numbers containing leading zeros, which can have base-related interpretation. For a beginner script, accept and validate simple decimal counters rather than arbitrary arithmetic expressions.

example.code:
sample_count=5
extra_count=2
total_count=$((sample_count+extra_count))
printf "Total samples: %s\n" "$total_count"
example.explanation: The result is 7. Arithmetic expansion is useful for counters, not a replacement for floating-point engineering calculations.

walkthrough: Assign a descriptive string and print it quoted.
Increment an integer counter.
Compare integer division with the expected real-number result.
Decide which settings may have defaults and which are required.
pitfalls: Putting spaces around = in an assignment.
Expecting floating-point division from Bash arithmetic.
Using familiar system variable names for unrelated counters.

exercises.title: Counter arithmetic
exercises.prompt: Compute the number of rows after adding two sample batches.
exercises.solution: total=$((first+second)); printf "%s\n" "$total". This models a count, so integer arithmetic is appropriate.
tests: Order of addition does not change the result.
exercises.extension: Add a third batch.

exercises.title: Document a default
exercises.prompt: Design behavior for an optional run label and a required input path.
exercises.inputs: No label supplied; input path supplied.
exercises.expected: Use a documented label fallback while retaining the explicit input path.
hints: Not every missing value should become empty text.
Treat required and optional inputs differently.
exercises.solution: Choose a fallback such as trial for the label; reject an absent input path with usage guidance before reading files.
tests: A missing required path fails clearly.
exercises.extension: Specify whether an empty label should trigger the default.

exercises.title: Choose the right tool
exercises.prompt: A script must average 5 and 2 to produce 3.5. Explain why a Bash-only arithmetic expression is a poor default.
exercises.expected: Delegate floating-point calculation to a suitable numerical tool.
hints: Integer division loses the fractional part.
exercises.solution: Bash can validate filenames and call a Python or MATLAB analysis. The numerical program should define parsing, precision, and error behavior.
tests: The expected mean is independently known.
The analysis output is checked before use.
exercises.extension: Define a simple input/output interface for the numerical program.

exercises.title: Assignment becomes a command
exercises.prompt: Diagnose sample_count = 5 in Bash.
exercises.expected: Bash attempts to execute a command named sample_count.
exercises.solution: Use sample_count=5. For arithmetic later use $((sample_count+1)); do not add spaces around the assignment operator.
exercises.extension: Contrast this with spaces inside a quoted string value.

review.question: What kind of arithmetic does Bash provide directly?
review.answer: Integer arithmetic, useful for counters and control flow.

review.question: When is a default dangerous?
review.answer: When it hides a missing required input and lets a script operate on an unintended file or assumption.

modules.title: Streams, redirection, and preserving raw data
modules.summary: Separate input, useful output, and diagnostics before building pipelines.
modules.why: A simulation run may produce both results and warnings. Mixing them can corrupt the next stage’s input.
explanation: A process normally has standard input, standard output, and standard error. Standard output is the ordinary result stream; standard error is where diagnostics often go. These are conventions that let programs cooperate. A numerical tool can print a machine-readable result on standard output while explaining a missing file on standard error.

Redirection changes where a stream goes. The > operator opens an output file and truncates an existing one before the command runs. Appending with >> preserves old content but can accumulate stale or duplicated results. Neither is automatically the correct choice. Decide whether a file is an immutable input, a per-run result, or an append-only journal before selecting the operator.

Never use the same file as both a pipeline’s input and its redirected output. The shell may truncate it before the first command reads anything. In these lessons, create tiny files only inside your scratch directory and write transformations to a different filename. Inspect the new file before any later replacement decision. Learning the timing of redirection prevents mistakes that otherwise look like mysterious data loss.

example.code:
printf "time_s,temperature_c
0,20
1,21
" > raw.csv
printf "Created a tiny practice fixture
" >&2
cat raw.csv > copied.csv
example.explanation: This creates raw.csv in the scratch directory and copies its content to a distinct generated file. Repeating the first line replaces this lesson fixture.

walkthrough: Create a small fixture in the scratch directory.
Send one result to stdout and one diagnostic to stderr.
Redirect stdout to a distinct output file.
Explain what repeating > and >> would do.
pitfalls: Reading and redirecting output to the same filename.
Appending results when a fresh per-run report was intended.
Sending diagnostic text into a data-only output stream.

exercises.title: Create a fixture
exercises.prompt: Write two lines into a new scratch file, then inspect them.
exercises.expected: A two-line file in the practice directory.
exercises.solution: printf "alpha\nbeta\n" > fixture.txt; cat fixture.txt. This intentionally creates or replaces only the named fixture.
tests: The content is not a single literal backslash-n string.
exercises.extension: Add a third line using a deliberate append.

exercises.title: Separate diagnostics
exercises.prompt: Design a script that emits 42 as its result and a progress message as a diagnostic.
exercises.inputs: One result and one status message.
exercises.solution: printf "42\n"; printf "Analysis complete\n" >&2. Run with stdout redirected to a scratch result file and inspect it.
tests: The result file contains no status sentence.
The diagnostic is still visible unless separately redirected.
exercises.extension: Capture stdout and stderr into separate files.

exercises.title: Choose overwrite or append
exercises.prompt: Specify file behavior for raw observations, a regenerated summary, and a study journal.
exercises.expected: Raw is preserved; summary gets a new per-run file or deliberate replacement; journal appends.
hints: Repeated runs must not silently duplicate summary rows.
exercises.solution: Document each policy before coding. Keep generated output paths separate from raw data and add run identifiers where needed.
tests: Re-running does not change raw data.
exercises.extension: Add an output-exists check to the summary workflow.

exercises.title: The empty input file
exercises.prompt: Explain why cat raw.csv > raw.csv can leave raw.csv empty.
exercises.inputs: The same path is input and redirected output.
exercises.expected: Redirection truncates the file before cat reads it.
hints: The shell sets up streams first.
exercises.solution: Write to a new file such as copied.csv instead and inspect it. Do not repeat the faulty command on real data to investigate.
tests: Input and output resolve to distinct paths.
exercises.extension: Draw the order: redirection, process start, file read.

review.question: What is stderr for?
review.answer: Diagnostics or other non-result output by convention, keeping stdout usable by another program.

review.question: When does > truncate a file?
review.answer: During shell redirection setup, before the command consumes its input.

modules.title: Pipelines and small text tools
modules.summary: Build a transformation one stage at a time and inspect the data between stages.
modules.why: A few composable tools can summarize simulation logs without creating a large custom application.
explanation: A pipeline connects one command’s standard output to another command’s standard input. The useful mental model is a sequence of transformations with an explicit data format at every boundary. Start by reading a tiny log, then filter lines, then count them. Inspect each intermediate result before compressing the work into one line.

Text tools have specific meanings. grep selects matching lines; wc -l counts newline characters, which corresponds to line count for the newline-terminated fixtures used here. sort orders text according to its options and locale. A numerical value represented as text is not automatically sorted numerically. These details matter when a report’s ranking or count influences what you investigate next.

Choose text tools for formats they actually understand. A simple line-oriented log is appropriate for grep. General CSV can contain quoted commas and embedded newlines, so splitting it with a basic delimiter command can corrupt records. Use a CSV-aware library for that case. Bash coordinates tools; it does not need to become a fragile replacement for a parser.

example.code:
printf "INFO start
WARN gap
INFO end
WARN stale
" | grep "^WARN" | wc -l
example.explanation: The result is 2. The fixture is deliberately line-oriented and newline-terminated.

walkthrough: Write a four-line synthetic log.
Run the filter alone and inspect matching lines.
Add the count only after the filter is correct.
Document the format assumptions that make the pipeline valid.
pitfalls: Counting substrings when you intend lines beginning with a severity.
Using lexical sort for numeric values.
Treating all comma-containing text as simple CSV.

exercises.title: Filter warnings
exercises.prompt: Print only lines beginning with WARN.
exercises.inputs: INFO start; WARN gap; INFO text says WARN; WARN stale, each on its own line.
exercises.expected: WARN gap and WARN stale only.
hints: Anchor the pattern at the line start.
exercises.solution: grep "^WARN" selects severity-prefixed lines. An unanchored WARN would also match the INFO sentence.
exercises.extension: Require a following space to avoid matching WARNING if the format demands it.

exercises.title: Count selected lines
exercises.prompt: Count ERROR severity lines in a newline-terminated fixture without including INFO mentions of ERROR.
exercises.inputs: ERROR read; INFO ERROR example; ERROR parse
exercises.solution: Use grep "^ERROR " followed by wc -l. Keep the fixture small enough to verify by inspection.
tests: No matching lines gives count zero.
A line containing the word later is excluded.
exercises.extension: Use grep -c and compare behavior and exit status.

exercises.title: Numeric ranking
exercises.prompt: Sort textual run durations from smallest to largest and explain the option choice.
hints: Default text ordering is not numeric ordering.
exercises.solution: sort -n interprets the leading numeric value for ordering. Define how malformed or missing durations will be handled before using real logs.
tests: Duplicate durations remain unless deliberately deduplicated.
