exercises.extension: Add run identifiers and define a stable numeric sort key.

exercises.title: A CSV parser made from cut
exercises.prompt: A script uses cut -d, on a CSV whose quoted notes contain commas. Explain why the selected field is wrong.
exercises.inputs: time,note,value with note such as "sensor, left".
exercises.expected: A simple comma split does not respect CSV quoting.
hints: The delimiter can occur inside a quoted field.
exercises.solution: Pass CSV processing to Python’s csv module or another documented CSV parser, while Bash handles filenames and orchestration.
tests: A quoted comma remains inside one field.
A newline inside a quoted field is handled if allowed by the data contract.
exercises.extension: Create a two-row regression fixture with quoted punctuation.

review.question: Why inspect intermediate pipeline output?
review.answer: It localizes mistakes and confirms the format passed between tools before another transformation hides it.

review.question: When should text processing move out of Bash?
review.answer: When structured parsing, complex validation, numerical arrays, or intricate data relationships exceed simple line-oriented transformations.

modules.title: Exit status and visible failure
modules.summary: Make success or failure part of the interface, not something inferred from a log message.
modules.why: A long simulation pipeline should not produce a convincing report after an earlier stage failed.
explanation: Every completed command returns an exit status. Zero conventionally means success, while nonzero values distinguish failure or other outcomes. Some tools use nonzero for an ordinary negative result, such as grep finding no match. Therefore you need the command’s documented contract rather than a blanket assumption that every nonzero result is a crash.

The special parameter $? holds the last command’s status, but another command replaces it. Capture it immediately or use the command directly in an if statement. A pipeline has its own status rules: by default its final command determines the pipeline status. Bash pipefail changes that rule so an earlier nonzero status can make the pipeline nonzero. It does not make every pipeline’s semantics automatically correct.

Do not add set -e and assume failure handling is solved. Context affects its behavior, and expected negative results can need explicit branches. For small learning scripts, clear if/else handling around important commands is easier to reason about. Decide what failure means, which outputs remain trustworthy, and what diagnostic should help the next person repair the input.

example.code:
if grep -q "^WARN " run.log; then
  printf "Warnings present\n"
else
  status=$?
  printf "grep status: %s\n" "$status" >&2
fi
example.explanation: For grep, status 1 means no selected lines; larger error statuses need different treatment. A production script should distinguish these cases explicitly.

walkthrough: Run one command that succeeds and one that returns nonzero.
Inspect the status immediately.
Write an explicit branch for an expected negative result.
Demonstrate how a final successful pipeline stage can hide an earlier failure.
pitfalls: Reading $? after a printf has already replaced it.
Treating grep’s no-match result as the same as a file-read error.
Assuming pipefail or set -e replaces an error-handling design.

exercises.title: Status immediately
exercises.prompt: Run true and false and record each status immediately.
hints: The words true and false here are commands.
exercises.solution: true; status=$?; printf "%s\n" "$status"; then repeat with false. The saved variable survives the print.
tests: The second test does not reuse the first saved value.
exercises.extension: Explain how an if statement avoids manual status capture.

exercises.title: No match is meaningful
exercises.prompt: Design three outcomes for grep: match, no match, and input error.
exercises.inputs: A readable log with a match, a readable log without one, and a missing path.
exercises.expected: Distinct result messages and failure handling.
hints: Do not collapse no data into bad data.
exercises.solution: Branch on 0 for match, 1 for no match, and other statuses for an error. Capture the status directly after grep.
tests: No-match is reported as an ordinary outcome.
Missing input prevents a success report.
exercises.extension: Have the script itself return a documented status.

exercises.title: Pipeline status experiment
exercises.prompt: Compare false | true with pipefail disabled and enabled in a scratch Bash session.
exercises.expected: Default pipeline status 0; with pipefail status nonzero.
exercises.solution: Observe the status in each mode and restore the session setting afterward if needed. Explain why this is a behavior experiment rather than an error policy.
exercises.extension: Repeat with true | false and explain why both modes fail.

exercises.title: The status was overwritten
exercises.prompt: A script runs an analyzer, prints "done", then tests $?. Diagnose why it reports success even when the analyzer failed.
exercises.solution: Use if analyzer; then ... else ... fi, or status=$? immediately after the analyzer. Do not print a success sentence before checking.
tests: A failing analyzer enters the failure branch.
A passing analyzer enters the success branch.
exercises.extension: Test the branch using a stub command.

review.question: What does exit status zero mean?
review.answer: It conventionally indicates success according to that command’s interface.

review.question: What is the default status of a pipeline?
review.answer: The status of its last command, unless options such as Bash pipefail change the rule.

modules.title: Script arguments and a clear usage contract
modules.summary: Turn an interactive command into a reusable script with deliberate input validation.
modules.why: A daily analysis should accept the file you intend rather than silently depend on the current folder or yesterday’s filename.
explanation: A script receives positional arguments. The first argument is $1, the count is $#, and the script name is available as $0. Before reading a positional parameter, check whether the required number of arguments was supplied. A short usage message is part of the interface: it should explain what input is required and what output the script produces.

Quoted argument forwarding preserves the original argument boundaries. A path containing spaces must remain one path through every wrapper layer. Do not concatenate arguments into a command string and then execute that string. Keeping program name and arguments separate is both simpler and more reliable. If the interface grows complicated, use a documented option parser rather than a pile of accidental conventions.

Validation should happen before work with side effects. Check argument count, file readability, and allowed mode values before starting a long analysis or creating a result. For this lesson the script only inspects a file, which keeps failures easy to test. Build a tiny fixture and deliberately omit the argument, provide a missing path, and provide a filename containing a space.

example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
if [[ $# -ne 1 ]]; then
  printf "Usage: inspect-log FILE\n" >&2
  exit 2
fi
if [[ ! -r "$1" ]]; then
  printf "Input is not readable\n" >&2
  exit 1
fi
wc -l < "$1"
example.explanation: Save as inspect-log.sh and run with bash inspect-log.sh "run one.log". It prints a line count for a readable newline-terminated file.

walkthrough: Write the usage sentence before the code.
Check argument count before accessing $1.
Validate the path and preserve its quoting.
Test normal, missing, and space-containing inputs.
pitfalls: Hard-coding yesterday’s filename.
Accessing missing arguments before validation.
Building a command string and using eval to run it.

exercises.title: Argument count
exercises.prompt: Write a script that requires exactly one argument and prints usage otherwise.
hints: Return a nonzero status for bad usage.
exercises.solution: Test [[ $# -ne 1 ]] and exit 2 with usage on stderr. Keep the expected interface visible.
exercises.extension: Include the script name in the usage text.

exercises.title: A path with spaces
exercises.prompt: Pass a file named run one.log to the line-count script.
exercises.inputs: A two-line fixture in the scratch directory.
exercises.solution: bash inspect-log.sh "run one.log" passes one argument; wc -l < "$1" reads the intended file.
tests: Neither run nor one.log is accessed separately.
exercises.extension: Try a path in a subdirectory with spaces.

exercises.title: Allowed modes
exercises.prompt: Design a script accepting MODE FILE, where MODE is either count or warnings. Validate before reading.
exercises.inputs: count fixture.log; warnings fixture.log; unknown fixture.log
exercises.expected: The first two operate; unknown is rejected with usage.
hints: Use a case statement for allowed modes.
exercises.solution: Reject unsupported mode text rather than treating it as a command name. Each supported branch invokes a fixed known operation.
tests: No mode text is executed as code.
exercises.extension: Add help as a documented third mode.

exercises.title: Argument forwarding splits names
exercises.prompt: A wrapper calls bash inspect-log.sh $1. Why can it fail for a valid path?
exercises.expected: Unquoted expansion can become multiple arguments.
hints: Preserve the argument boundary at every layer.
The called script’s validation reveals the split.
exercises.solution: Use bash inspect-log.sh "$1". For forwarding all original arguments, use quoted "$@" after validating the wrapper’s own interface.
tests: The path reaches the child unchanged.
An empty argument is not silently dropped.
exercises.extension: Explain why "$*" is not interchangeable with "$@".

review.question: Why validate argument count first?
review.answer: It prevents missing values from being mistaken for legitimate input and provides a clear usage failure.

review.question: What does quoted "$@" preserve?
review.answer: Each original positional argument as its own argument, including spaces and empty values.

modules.title: Conditionals that express the workflow
modules.summary: Make branch decisions explicit using file tests, string choices, and numeric comparisons.
modules.why: A robust run script needs to know whether an input exists, a mode is supported, and a prerequisite succeeded.
explanation: A conditional is a choice based on a command’s success or an expression’s truth. In Bash, [[ ... ]] provides a useful expression form for many checks. A readable-file test answers a different question from a nonempty-string test, and neither proves that a CSV’s contents are valid. Match the test to the decision rather than treating any nonempty value as evidence of correctness.

Use case for a small set of named modes. It makes the allowed vocabulary visible and avoids evaluating user-supplied text as a command. For numeric comparisons, validate the expected numeric representation before arithmetic. Bash arithmetic is not an appropriate parser for arbitrary untrusted expressions, and lexical string ordering is different from numeric ordering.

Keep branches short and meaningful. A branch should explain what happens when a condition is false, not only the happy path. Avoid compact chains that look like if/else but behave differently when the middle command fails. Readability matters because a future failed simulation may require you to diagnose the workflow quickly, under less convenient conditions than a tutorial.

example.explanation: The accepted modes are explicit. The mode string is compared as data, never executed as a command.

walkthrough: List the possible states of the input.
Choose a test that answers exactly the intended question.
Write an explicit failure branch.
Test every branch with a tiny fixture.
pitfalls: Assuming a readable file contains valid data.
Comparing numeric text with lexical operators.
Using a && b || c as if c could never run after a succeeds.

exercises.title: Readable input
exercises.prompt: Check whether a supplied path is readable and print an appropriate message.
exercises.inputs: A readable fixture and a missing path.
exercises.expected: Different branches for readable and unavailable input.
exercises.solution: if [[ -r "$path" ]]; then ... else ... fi. Keep a later content validator separate.
tests: A malformed but readable file still passes this access check.
exercises.extension: Add a regular-file test if directories are not allowed.

exercises.title: Named operation
exercises.prompt: Implement count and inspect modes with a default rejection branch.
exercises.expected: Only the two documented values are accepted.
exercises.solution: case "$mode" in count) ... ;; inspect) ... ;; *) ... ;; esac. Fixed operations are selected by the data value.
tests: Each supported mode reaches its own branch.
exercises.extension: Add a mode that prints help without reading files.

exercises.title: Validate a positive count
exercises.prompt: Specify a decimal positive-integer contract for a sample count before using it in a loop.
hints: Representation and range are separate checks.
Do not feed arbitrary expressions into arithmetic.
exercises.solution: First require digits in the intended format, then enforce a positive range. Document a reasonable maximum to avoid accidental enormous work.
exercises.extension: Decide whether leading zeros are accepted and normalize them explicitly.

exercises.title: The misleading compact chain
exercises.prompt: A script uses validate && analyze || report_invalid. Why might report_invalid run even after validation succeeds?
exercises.expected: The final branch responds to the failed analyze command.
hints: This is not a complete if/else substitute.
exercises.solution: Use if validate; then if analyze; then ... else report_analysis_failure; fi; else report_invalid; fi. Distinguish the two failures.
tests: Validation failure has its own message.
Analysis failure is not mislabeled as invalid input.
exercises.extension: Refactor the nested branch into small functions.

review.question: Does -r validate the contents of a file?
review.answer: No. It checks readability; the data format and scientific validity need separate checks.

review.question: Why use case for modes?
review.answer: It exposes a finite set of accepted values and keeps input as data instead of executable text.

modules.title: Loops over records, not accidental words
modules.summary: Repeat work while preserving the boundaries of filenames and text lines.
modules.why: Batch processing is one of Bash’s best uses, provided each item remains intact.
explanation: A loop repeats an operation for a sequence of items. The crucial question is what counts as an item. A list of filenames is not safely represented by arbitrary whitespace-separated text, because a filename can itself contain spaces. Similarly, a line of a log may contain several words that must remain one record.

For a fixed list, quote each item and quote the loop variable when passing it to commands. For lines from a simple text file, IFS= read -r preserves leading and trailing whitespace and backslashes. A redirected while loop can keep its state in the current shell, unlike common pipeline-loop forms that may execute in a subshell. Learn this difference with a counter before relying on it in a report.

Start by printing the work you intend to perform. Once the item boundaries and count are correct, replace the print with a known read-only transformation. Record a per-item result and decide what should happen if one item fails. A batch that processes nine files and silently skips the tenth is not a complete successful analysis.

example.code:
count=0
while IFS= read -r line; do
  printf "<%s>\n" "$line"
  count=$((count+1))
done < records.txt
printf "Records: %s\n" "$count"
example.explanation: This assumes a newline-terminated records.txt fixture. The redirection avoids placing the loop in a pipeline subshell.

walkthrough: Create three newline-terminated records, including a space and a backslash.
Print each record with visible delimiters.
Count iterations and inspect the counter after the loop.
Define a policy for an input file whose last line lacks a newline.
pitfalls: Using for line in $(cat file), which splits on words.
Dropping backslashes by omitting read -r.
Expecting a pipeline subshell’s counter to update the parent shell.

exercises.title: Fixed list
exercises.prompt: Loop over two names, one containing a space, and print one bracketed name per line.
hints: Quote the expansion inside the loop.
exercises.solution: for name in "alpha" "rover run"; do printf "[%s]\n" "$name"; done.
tests: The space remains inside the second name.
exercises.extension: Add an empty-string item and observe that it remains an item.

exercises.title: Preserve text lines
exercises.prompt: Read a three-line fixture without splitting words or interpreting backslashes.
exercises.inputs: alpha beta; path\segment; final, each newline-terminated.
exercises.solution: while IFS= read -r line; do printf "%s\n" "$line"; done < records.txt. This contract expects newline-terminated records.
exercises.extension: Support a final unterminated record explicitly.

exercises.title: Batch outcome summary
exercises.prompt: Design a loop that reports how many files succeeded and failed without hiding individual failures.
exercises.inputs: Three fixtures, one deliberately unreadable or absent.
exercises.expected: Two successes and one failure under the defined test.
hints: Store success and failure counters separately.
exercises.solution: Use an if around each file operation, increment the appropriate count, and print a final summary. Return a failure status when the batch contract requires all files.
tests: A failed item cannot be counted as successful.
exercises.extension: Add a separate list of failed paths for retry.

exercises.title: Counter disappears
exercises.prompt: A counter incremented inside cat records.txt | while read ... remains zero afterward. Explain a likely cause.
exercises.expected: The loop may run in a subshell whose variables do not update the parent.
hints: Feed the loop with input redirection instead.
exercises.solution: Use while ...; done < records.txt for this simple file case. Then the counter is available in the surrounding shell.
tests: The final count equals the number of records.
Input boundaries are still preserved with IFS= read -r.
exercises.extension: Explain why a subshell can be useful when intentional.

review.question: Why avoid for line in $(cat file)?
review.answer: Command substitution and word splitting do not preserve arbitrary line boundaries or filename characters.

review.question: What does read -r prevent?
review.answer: It prevents read from treating backslashes as escape characters.

modules.title: Arrays and file discovery
modules.summary: Keep an argument list structured and inspect discovered files before processing them.
modules.why: A reproducible batch needs an exact list of inputs, including paths containing spaces.
explanation: An array stores separate elements without forcing you to encode them into one space-separated string. This makes it suitable for a command’s arguments or a small list of files. Quoted expansion of all array elements preserves those boundaries. It is a better design than building a string with embedded quote marks and hoping Bash will parse it again.

File discovery introduces another boundary problem. A newline-separated listing is convenient for human inspection but cannot represent every possible filename unambiguously. A NUL-delimited stream is suitable for machine handling because filenames cannot contain that delimiter. GNU find supports -print0, and compatible consumers can preserve each complete path. Use a read-only listing first to verify the selection criteria.

Keep the discovery scope narrow. Start from the project’s input directory, filter regular files and the intended suffix, and record which files were selected. An empty match set deserves an explicit outcome, especially when the absence of logs could otherwise look like a successful zero-error run. The exercises here only list and inspect files; they do not bulk rename or delete anything.

example.code:
files=("run one.log" "run two.log")
for file in "${files[@]}"; do
  printf "Input: <%s>\n" "$file"
done
example.explanation: Each array element remains one argument, including its space. The quoted @ expansion is the important boundary-preserving step.

walkthrough: Create an array of two space-containing names.
Print each element and count the results.
Use find on a scratch input folder with a quoted pattern.
Decide how an empty selection should be reported.
pitfalls: Storing many paths in one string.
Parsing ls output as a machine-readable file list.
Letting the shell expand a find pattern before find receives it.

exercises.title: Array boundaries
exercises.prompt: Store three input names in an indexed Bash array and print them individually.
hints: Use parentheses for the array assignment.
exercises.solution: files=("a.log" "run one.log" "z.log"); for file in "${files[@]}"; do printf "%s\n" "$file"; done.
tests: The middle name is not split.
exercises.extension: Add an empty element and inspect its behavior.

exercises.title: Discover only logs
exercises.prompt: List regular .log files below a scratch inputs directory.
exercises.inputs: Mixed .log and .csv files plus a subdirectory.
exercises.expected: Only regular files whose names end in .log.
exercises.solution: find ./inputs -type f -name "*.log" -print. The quoted glob belongs to find rather than the parent shell.
tests: A directory named archive.log is excluded.
A file named notes.csv is excluded.
exercises.extension: Repeat with -print0 for a machine consumer.

exercises.title: Machine-safe discovery
exercises.prompt: Design a NUL-delimited loop that prints discovered paths with boundaries intact.
exercises.expected: Every selected file is processed exactly once.
hints: Use a consumer that reads NUL delimiters.
exercises.solution: In Bash, use while IFS= read -r -d "" file; do printf "<%s>\n" "$file"; done < <(find ./inputs -type f -name "*.log" -print0). This is Bash-specific process substitution.
tests: An empty folder produces zero iterations.
exercises.extension: Add an explicit empty-selection report.

exercises.title: A glob expanded too early
exercises.prompt: Why can find ./inputs -name *.log behave differently depending on files in the current directory?
exercises.expected: The shell may expand the pattern before find sees it.
hints: There are two different pattern interpreters involved.
Choose which one owns the glob.
exercises.solution: Use -name "*.log" so find receives the literal pattern. The discovery should not depend on unrelated matching files in the caller’s current directory.
tests: Behavior is stable when the caller has matching files.
Only the intended search root is traversed.
exercises.extension: Describe the same problem with an unquoted grep pattern.

review.question: Why use an array for command arguments?
review.answer: It preserves separate values directly, including spaces and empty elements, without reparsing a string as code.

review.question: Why is NUL useful for filename lists?
review.answer: It separates filenames unambiguously because a filename cannot contain a NUL character.

modules.title: Functions with small responsibilities
modules.summary: Give repeated workflow steps a name and a clear status contract.
modules.why: A script becomes easier to test when discovery, validation, analysis, and reporting are separate steps.
explanation: A shell function is a named group of commands that runs in the shell context. It receives positional arguments and returns an exit status. It does not return an arbitrary string through return; use standard output for a data result and the status for success or failure. This distinction helps functions compose with ordinary command-line tools.

Use local variables inside functions to avoid accidentally changing unrelated script state. Validate the function’s inputs and preserve quoted argument boundaries exactly as in a script. Keep diagnostics on standard error if standard output is intended to be captured. A function named count_records should not also rename files or change the caller’s working directory without an explicit contract.

Choose functions around responsibilities rather than line counts. A five-line validator can be worth naming because it describes a meaningful decision. Avoid introducing layers that only obscure a simple command. Your goal is a script that reads like a sequence of clear steps and whose failures point to a specific boundary. Start by testing functions against tiny fixtures before running them across a large folder.

example.explanation: The function emits a line count on stdout and returns nonzero if the input is not readable. Callers should supply exactly one argument or add count validation.

walkthrough: Name one repeated responsibility.
Define inputs, stdout format, and status behavior.
Use local variables and quote paths.
Test the function directly before integrating it.
pitfalls: Trying to return a large numerical result through an exit status.
Printing progress messages into captured data output.
Changing global variables accidentally.

exercises.title: A validation function
exercises.prompt: Write a function that succeeds only when its one argument is a readable regular file.
exercises.inputs: One existing fixture and one missing path.
exercises.expected: Status 0 for the valid file, nonzero otherwise.
exercises.solution: Use [[ $# -eq 1 ]] before inspecting $1, then [[ -f "$1" && -r "$1" ]]. The final test supplies the status.
exercises.extension: Add a diagnostic without changing the status contract.

exercises.title: Data through stdout
exercises.prompt: Write a function that prints a supplied label in a stable format while leaving status for success.
exercises.solution: A function can printf "label=%s\n" "$1". Do not use return "$1"; return is for numeric status.
exercises.extension: Capture the output into a variable and inspect it.

exercises.title: No hidden directory changes
exercises.prompt: Refactor a function that changes into an input directory and forgets to change back.
exercises.inputs: Caller expects its current directory unchanged.
exercises.expected: The function’s effect is isolated or removed.
hints: A subshell can intentionally contain cd.
exercises.solution: Use explicit file paths, or perform the directory-specific work in a subshell. Document any unavoidable state changes.
tests: The intended file is still accessed.
exercises.extension: Add a test for failure during the internal operation.

exercises.title: Debug text corrupts a number
exercises.prompt: A caller captures count=$(count_lines file), but the function prints "starting" and then the number. Diagnose the broken interface.
exercises.expected: Send diagnostics to stderr or remove them from the data function.
exercises.solution: Use printf "starting\n" >&2 for a diagnostic, and only the count on stdout. Also check the function’s exit status before using the data.
tests: Captured output contains only the number.
Failure does not produce a misleading valid count.
exercises.extension: Document whether leading whitespace from wc is normalized.

review.question: What does return communicate in a shell function?
review.answer: An exit status, conventionally zero for success and nonzero for failure, not an arbitrary data value.

review.question: Why declare local variables?
review.answer: To limit accidental changes to the surrounding script’s state and make the function’s dependencies clearer.

modules.title: Test scripts with awkward fixtures
modules.summary: Verify success, failure, quoting, and output contracts before processing real project data.
modules.why: The most useful shell tests often expose problems that an ordinary filename and perfect input would never reveal.
explanation: A script test should check more than whether a command ran. Inspect its exit status, standard output, standard error, and file effects. A program that reports success but writes the wrong file has failed its contract. Build small fixtures where the correct answer is obvious and include one missing file, one empty file, and one path containing a space.

Static analysis catches another class of mistakes. ShellCheck can identify many suspicious expansions, quoting errors, and portability issues without running the script. Read its explanation rather than silencing warnings mechanically. A static warning is evidence to investigate, and a clean report is not a proof of correctness. Runtime behavior, data meaning, and intended side effects still require tests.

Keep test data inside a fresh temporary directory and avoid destructive cleanup logic in beginner exercises. A test harness can report its scratch location for inspection. Introduce one deliberate defect, confirm a test fails, repair it, and rerun. This demonstrates that the test is capable of detecting the behavior you care about instead of merely echoing a reassuring message.

example.code:
if bash inspect-log.sh "missing-fixture.log" > actual.out 2> actual.err; then
  printf "FAIL: missing input was accepted\n"
else
  printf "PASS: missing input was rejected\n"
fi
example.explanation: Run in a scratch directory. The harness checks the failure path and saves both streams for inspection.

walkthrough: List the script’s observable contract.
Create ordinary, empty, missing, and space-containing fixtures.
Check status, output, diagnostics, and files separately.
Run ShellCheck and investigate relevant findings.
pitfalls: Testing only the successful case.
Calling every nonzero status a test failure when the case expects rejection.
Suppressing static warnings without understanding them.

exercises.title: Known-count fixture
exercises.prompt: Test the line-count script with exactly three newline-terminated records.
exercises.inputs: A scratch file containing a, b, c.
exercises.solution: Run the script, save stdout, check the exit status, and compare the normalized count with 3.
tests: Adding a fourth changes the expected count.
exercises.extension: Add an empty-file test expecting zero.

exercises.title: Expected rejection
exercises.prompt: Test that a missing input produces a nonzero status and a helpful diagnostic.
exercises.inputs: A path guaranteed absent in the new scratch directory.
exercises.expected: No success result; nonzero status; nonempty stderr.
hints: The test passes when the script rejects the input.
Do not confuse the test status with the script status.
exercises.solution: Wrap the script in an if and invert the test expectation. Inspect actual.err for the diagnostic.
tests: No result file is mistaken for valid analysis.
The error explains which condition failed.
exercises.extension: Distinguish bad usage from missing-file status codes.

exercises.title: Quoting regression
exercises.prompt: Create a fixture path with spaces and confirm the script handles it exactly like an ordinary path.
hints: Quote the path in the harness too.
A broken harness can mimic a broken script.
exercises.solution: Compare ordinary and awkward names containing identical data. Their outputs and statuses should agree.
tests: Exactly one path argument reaches the script.
exercises.extension: Add a leading-dash basename with an explicit ./ path.

exercises.title: A test that cannot fail
exercises.prompt: A harness prints PASS after running the script but never checks its result. Explain why it provides no evidence.
exercises.inputs: The script may return any status.
exercises.expected: PASS must depend on an asserted outcome.
hints: Find the condition controlling the message.
exercises.solution: Check the expected status and output before printing PASS. A deliberate defect should change the harness result.
exercises.extension: Give the harness its own nonzero exit status when any assertion fails.

review.question: What should a shell test observe?
review.answer: Status, stdout, stderr, and intended file effects, according to the script’s contract.

review.question: What does ShellCheck add?
review.answer: Static detection and explanation of many suspicious shell patterns; it complements rather than replaces behavioral tests.

modules.title: Git as an experiment notebook
modules.summary: Track source changes with small meaningful commits and inspect what is actually recorded.
modules.why: A future result is easier to explain when you can identify the exact code version that produced it.
explanation: Git records snapshots of selected files. The working tree is what you are editing, the staging area is what the next commit will contain, and a commit is a saved snapshot with a message and parent history. These are distinct states. Editing a file after staging it does not automatically update the staged content.

Use read-only inspection habitually: status shows what changed, diff shows unstaged changes, and diff --cached shows the staged changes. Review before committing so generated outputs, accidental large files, or private configuration do not enter the history unintentionally. A useful commit message describes a coherent change and its purpose, such as adding a missing-input check.

A local repository does not require publishing anything. Practice with a tiny scratch project before using a remote. Git history is not a complete backup plan, and ignoring a file does not remove it from earlier commits. For engineering work, record code revision, input identity, and environment together; a commit alone does not identify a measurement file stored somewhere else.

example.code:
git status --short
git diff
git diff --cached
git log -5 --oneline
example.explanation: Run inside a repository. These commands inspect state and history without changing it.

walkthrough: Create or use a dedicated practice repository.
Edit a small text source file and inspect the unstaged diff.
Stage only the intended file and inspect the staged diff.
Commit a coherent change and inspect its history.
pitfalls: Confusing staged content with the latest working-tree contents.
Treating .gitignore as removal from existing history.
Publishing private configuration as part of a broad add operation.

exercises.title: Three states
exercises.prompt: Explain where an edit lives before staging, after staging, and after committing.
exercises.expected: Working tree; staging area snapshot; commit history.
hints: A later edit can coexist with an earlier staged version.
exercises.solution: Use git status and the two diff forms to inspect each boundary. Describe what the next commit would contain.
tests: Unstaged changes appear in git diff.
Staged changes appear in git diff --cached.
exercises.extension: Stage, edit again, and explain both diffs.

exercises.title: A focused commit
exercises.prompt: In a practice repository, add one clear input-validation change and commit only the intended file.
exercises.inputs: A small script and unrelated notes edit.
exercises.expected: The commit contains the script change, not unrelated notes.
exercises.solution: Use git add with the specific file, inspect git diff --cached, then commit a message explaining the validation behavior.
tests: Unrelated notes remain outside the commit.
The commit diff matches the intended change.
exercises.extension: Include the relevant test in the same coherent commit.

exercises.title: Run provenance
exercises.prompt: Design a small metadata record linking a result to code and input identity.
exercises.inputs: A code revision, input filename/checksum, tool versions.
exercises.expected: A future reader can identify the producing code and data.
hints: A commit does not identify untracked data.
exercises.solution: Store the commit identifier, whether local edits existed, input checksum, run arguments, and relevant versions with the result.
tests: Two changed inputs have distinguishable records.
Uncommitted code is not represented as a clean revision.
exercises.extension: Add a short interpretation of the result.

exercises.title: Changed after staging
exercises.prompt: A file was staged, then corrected, then committed without staging again. Why is the correction absent from the commit?
exercises.inputs: The staging area retained an earlier snapshot.
exercises.expected: Stage the intended corrected content after inspection.
hints: Working-tree edits do not automatically alter it.
exercises.solution: Inspect both diffs, stage the corrected file, and review the staged diff again before committing.
tests: The final staged diff includes the correction.
exercises.extension: Explain this behavior with a three-column diagram.

review.question: What does git diff --cached show?
review.answer: The staged changes that would enter the next commit relative to the current commit.

review.question: Is a commit enough to reproduce a scientific result?
review.answer: No. Inputs, environment, run arguments, and any uncommitted changes also matter.

modules.title: Environment and reproducible configuration
modules.summary: Make tool selection and run settings visible without exposing private values.
modules.why: The same script can behave differently when it finds another interpreter, locale, or dependency version.
explanation: A process inherits an environment containing named string values. Some variables affect command lookup, locale, or library behavior. A script should document the settings it relies on rather than assuming every terminal starts identically. Use command -v to inspect which executable will run and the tool’s documented version option to record its identity.

Keep run configuration separate from secrets. A sample configuration can show expected names and harmless defaults without containing credentials. Do not print the whole environment into a public report, because it may include private values. For a learning pipeline, record only a small allowlist of relevant non-sensitive settings such as tool versions and explicitly chosen locale behavior.

Reproducibility also includes platform assumptions. GNU and BSD tools may offer different flags, Bash versions may differ, and PowerShell is not Bash. State the environment you tested and prefer simple interfaces where practical. If a task requires sophisticated environment management, learn it when the project earns that complexity rather than collecting tools without a use case.

example.code:
command -v bash
command -v python3
bash --version
LC_ALL=C sort durations.txt
example.explanation: The locale assignment applies to this sort invocation. It is useful when a workflow requires predictable byte-oriented ordering, but must match the data’s intended interpretation.

walkthrough: Identify each executable used by the script.
Record only relevant non-sensitive versions/settings.
Document platform-specific flags.
Run from a fresh shell and compare behavior.
pitfalls: Dumping the entire environment into logs.
Assuming every sort order is independent of locale.
Confusing interpreter availability with matching dependency versions.

exercises.title: Executable identity
exercises.prompt: Find which python3 executable the shell will invoke.
exercises.inputs: A Bash environment with or without python3.
exercises.expected: A resolved path or a documented missing-command outcome.
hints: Do not infer from an application icon.
exercises.solution: Record command -v python3 and, if present, its version using the documented option. This identifies the executable in this environment.
tests: The recorded path matches the intended environment.
exercises.extension: Compare an interactive shell and a project launcher.

exercises.title: Local configuration
exercises.prompt: Define a harmless run label and output folder as explicit script inputs rather than hidden global assumptions.
exercises.inputs: run label trialA; output folder results/trialA.
exercises.expected: The selected values are visible in the run summary.
exercises.solution: Validate the configuration at startup and print only non-sensitive values useful for reproducing the run.
tests: A missing required value fails clearly.
exercises.extension: Provide an example config containing no private values.

exercises.title: Portability note
exercises.prompt: Write a compatibility section for a script using Bash arrays and GNU find -print0.
exercises.inputs: The script is intended for a tested Linux Bash environment.
exercises.expected: The note names tested tools and avoids claiming POSIX-sh portability.
hints: Language and tool interfaces are separate dependencies.
List flags that need verification elsewhere.
exercises.solution: Document the Bash version family, GNU utility assumptions, and a small smoke-test command. Test another platform before claiming support.
tests: Running under sh is not recommended accidentally.
A missing dependency is detected early.
exercises.extension: Replace one platform-specific operation with a verified portable alternative.

exercises.title: The wrong interpreter
exercises.prompt: An interactive command uses the desired Python environment, but a scheduled or fresh-shell run finds a different interpreter. Diagnose the likely boundary.
exercises.expected: Make interpreter selection explicit and verify it at startup.
hints: Do not assume shell startup files ran.
exercises.solution: Document and invoke the intended environment through its supported mechanism. Record version identity with each run and avoid hard-coded private machine paths in shared examples.
tests: The two contexts identify the same intended interpreter.
exercises.extension: Add a startup dependency check.

review.question: Why avoid printing the entire environment?
review.answer: It can contain private or irrelevant values; an allowlist records useful provenance without unnecessary disclosure.

review.question: Why is command -v useful?
review.answer: It shows how the current shell resolves a command, helping identify environment-dependent tool selection.

modules.title: Processes, waiting, and truthful completion
modules.summary: Understand when work has actually finished before consuming its output.
modules.why: Simulation orchestration can fail when a report begins while the solver is still running.
explanation: A foreground command normally completes before the shell continues to the next command. Appending & starts work asynchronously, allowing the shell to continue sooner. This can be useful, but it introduces a dependency problem: the output file may not be complete when another step tries to read it.

Capture the process identifier of a background job you started and use wait to observe its completion and status. Do not infer completion from a file merely existing, because a process may create the file before finishing or fail after writing part of it. For a first workflow, sequential execution is often easier to verify than parallel execution.

Interactive job control, process identifiers, and long-lived services are related but distinct topics. This lesson uses a harmless short process that you own. Do not experiment by stopping unrelated system processes. For later simulations, define cancellation, timeout, logging, and partial-output policies explicitly. Faster orchestration is only useful when the dependencies and outcomes remain understandable.

example.code:
sleep 1 &
job_pid=$!
if wait "$job_pid"; then
  printf "Owned job completed successfully\n"
else
  printf "Owned job failed\n" >&2
fi
example.explanation: This starts and waits for a harmless short process. The completion message follows wait, not merely process launch.

walkthrough: Run a short command in the foreground.
Run the same harmless command in the background.
Capture its identifier and wait for it.
Make the next step conditional on successful completion.
pitfalls: Treating process launch as successful completion.
Reading a file while its producer is still writing.
Managing a process you did not start or identify.

exercises.title: Foreground order
exercises.prompt: Predict output order for a print, a short foreground sleep, and another print.
exercises.expected: before appears first, after appears only after the sleep completes.
hints: Do not equate delay with a hang.
exercises.solution: The shell waits for the foreground process before executing the next command. Observe once using harmless prints.
exercises.extension: Contrast with background execution.

exercises.title: Wait for owned work
exercises.prompt: Start sleep 1 in the background, capture its PID, and print completion after wait succeeds.
exercises.expected: Completion is reported after the process exits.
hints: $! identifies the most recent asynchronous job.
exercises.solution: Use job_pid=$! immediately after launching, then if wait "$job_pid"; then ... fi.
tests: The stored PID is not overwritten by another launch.
exercises.extension: Add a second owned job and wait for both separately.

exercises.title: Dependency plan
exercises.prompt: Design a three-step pipeline: generate samples, analyze samples, render report. Identify which steps may overlap.
exercises.inputs: Analysis depends on complete samples; report depends on analysis.
exercises.expected: The core chain is sequential unless a dependency is removed deliberately.
hints: File existence is not sufficient readiness.
exercises.solution: Require successful producer completion before each consumer. Independent metadata collection might overlap, but must not change the data dependency.
tests: A failed analysis prevents a success report.
exercises.extension: Add an explicit partial-output policy.

exercises.title: Premature success
exercises.prompt: A script launches analyzer & and immediately prints "analysis complete". Explain the false claim.
exercises.expected: The message proves launch only, not completion.
exercises.solution: Capture the job PID, wait for it, and print success only after a successful exit. Keep failures visible and do not consume incomplete output.
tests: A failing analyzer produces no success message.
A slow analyzer delays the completion message.
exercises.extension: Test with a stub that exits nonzero.

review.question: What does & change?
review.answer: It starts a command asynchronously so the shell can continue before the command finishes.

review.question: Why is file existence a weak completion signal?
review.answer: The file may be incomplete, stale, or left by a failed producer.

modules.title: Build a rerunnable experiment pipeline
modules.summary: Connect validation, analysis, provenance, and reporting into one transparent workflow.
modules.why: The lasting value of shell scripting is making a useful experiment repeatable after weeks or years away.
explanation: A rerunnable pipeline has a defined input set, known tools, an explicit order, and a clear output contract. Begin with one file and one analysis command. Add validation and a small test fixture before scaling to a folder. The top-level script should read like a short explanation of the workflow rather than a puzzle of nested one-liners.

Choose what happens on rerun. A unique per-run output directory avoids confusing old results with new ones. A deliberate overwrite policy can also work for generated artifacts, but it must never target the raw observations. Record arguments, code revision, relevant versions, and input identity. A checksum helps distinguish changed bytes; it is not a statement about scientific quality.

At the end, verify the expected outputs rather than merely reaching the final line. Did every selected input get an outcome? Is the result parseable, nonempty when required, and associated with the current run? Write a short limitations note. Your first pipeline might summarize invented rover logs; later the same structure can coordinate MATLAB models, Python analysis, and simulator outputs without hiding their assumptions.

example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
if [[ $# -ne 1 || ! -r "$1" ]]; then
  printf "Usage: summarize READABLE_LOG\n" >&2
  exit 2
fi
printf "Input: %s\n" "$1"
if wc -l < "$1"; then
  printf "Line-count step completed\n" >&2
else
  printf "Line-count step failed\n" >&2
  exit 1
fi
example.explanation: This is a deliberately small starting pipeline. Expand it only after defining and testing each additional boundary.

walkthrough: Write the workflow contract in a README.
Validate before running analysis.
Record a per-run manifest and keep raw data unchanged.
Verify outputs and report both successes and failures.
pitfalls: Reusing a stale output after a failed run.
Declaring success because the script reached its end.
Growing a shell script into an undocumented data-processing language.

exercises.title: Workflow contract
exercises.prompt: Write the input, output, success, and failure contract for a log-summary script.
exercises.expected: A reader knows what counts are produced and what invalid input does.
hints: Specify the format, not just the filename.
exercises.solution: Document required file readability, severity-line format, count outputs, status codes, and preservation of the source log.
tests: An empty input has a defined meaning.
A missing input has a different outcome.
exercises.extension: Add an example fixture and expected summary.

exercises.title: Fresh outputs
exercises.prompt: Design a per-run output directory policy that prevents old results from masquerading as current results.
exercises.inputs: Two executions with different input logs.
exercises.expected: Each run has a distinct identifiable result set.
hints: Validate the target before creating results.
exercises.solution: Require a new run directory or reject an existing one under the chosen policy. Store a manifest alongside generated artifacts.
tests: The second run cannot silently read the first summary.
Raw inputs remain outside the generated output folder.
exercises.extension: Add a human-readable summary of the run.

exercises.title: Cross-language orchestration
exercises.prompt: Plan Bash validation followed by Python analysis and MATLAB comparison, using CSV as an explicit interface.
exercises.expected: Each stage has a documented format, status check, and evidence artifact.
hints: Check the producer before invoking its consumer.
exercises.solution: Validate filenames and tool availability, run the producer, inspect its status, validate the output schema, then run the comparison. Record versions and assumptions.
tests: A schema mismatch is reported explicitly.
exercises.extension: Add a small end-to-end fixture with a known answer.

exercises.title: Stale success artifact
exercises.prompt: A script reads summary.csv after analysis fails; the file was left by yesterday’s run. Why is existence checking insufficient?
exercises.expected: Associate outputs with the current successful run.
exercises.solution: Stop on analysis failure and use a new run directory or a verified current-run marker. A stale file should never satisfy the new run’s success contract.
tests: A failing run cannot publish yesterday’s result.
The manifest identifies the current inputs.
exercises.extension: Test this case deliberately in a scratch directory.

review.question: What makes a pipeline rerunnable?
review.answer: Explicit inputs and environment, controlled output policy, checked dependencies, and enough provenance to reproduce the result.

review.question: When should a shell pipeline call another language?
review.answer: When structured parsing, numerical analysis, complex data models, or detailed testing is clearer in a dedicated programming language.

projects.title: The rover mass and energy ledger
projects.summary: Build a small command-line engineering ledger that makes units, assumptions, and missing information visible. Start with invented component data, then use measured values from a harmless desktop build.

milestones.title: Define the component schema
milestones.deliverable: A CSV containing component_id, mass_kg, average_power_w, and a note describing the power assumption.
milestones.acceptance: Every row has a unique ID; masses and power values are finite and nonnegative; invalid rows receive explicit reasons.

milestones.title: Compute transparent totals
milestones.deliverable: A summary with total mass, total assumed power, and ideal energy for a specified duration.
milestones.acceptance: A hand-checked three-component fixture matches exactly or within documented floating-point tolerance. The ideal model is labeled.

milestones.title: Make the interface repeatable
milestones.deliverable: A CLI accepting input, duration, and output path.
milestones.acceptance: --help states units; changing duration does not require source edits; the input file remains unchanged.

milestones.title: Prepare a useful design review
milestones.deliverable: A short report comparing two component selections and listing omitted effects.
milestones.acceptance: The report distinguishes measured, manufacturer-stated, and assumed quantities and does not claim actual battery runtime from an ideal constant-power estimate.

testPlan: Zero components produces a documented empty-ledger response.
Duplicate component IDs are rejected.
A negative mass or non-finite power is reported.
Doubling duration doubles ideal energy without changing mass.
extensions: Add uncertainty ranges as explicitly assumed scenarios.
Compare alternative component selections.
Create a plot of mass contribution by component.
portfolio: README with the physical question and unit conventions.
One comparison report with assumptions and limitations.
A note explaining what real measurements would improve the estimate.
constraints: No optimization claim without a defined objective and constraints.
No hardware purchase or physical robot is required.
Keep the model simple enough to verify by hand.

projects.title: A telemetry quality station
projects.summary: Turn messy environmental logs into an auditable quality report, a clean dataset, and figures that preserve evidence of missingness.

milestones.title: Create a deliberate fixture
milestones.deliverable: A synthetic CSV containing valid rows, a missing field, a duplicate timestamp, a non-finite value, and a time gap.
milestones.acceptance: The fixture has a written answer key stating each expected issue before the parser is implemented.

milestones.title: Validate without erasing history
milestones.deliverable: A validator returning accepted records and a separate issue table with source row references.
milestones.acceptance: No invalid row silently becomes zero; the raw file is preserved; accepted and rejected counts reconcile with total input.

milestones.title: Build an honest summary
milestones.deliverable: Per-sensor counts, interval coverage, min/max, mean/median, and timestamp-gap information.
milestones.acceptance: Every statistic states its contributing count and unit. Empty groups produce an explicit absence rather than a fabricated result.

milestones.title: Publish a reproducible report
milestones.deliverable: A time-history figure, gap annotations, issue CSV, manifest, and a short interpretation.
milestones.acceptance: One command recreates all outputs from the fixture. The interpretation separates measurement, estimate, and unknown.

testPlan: All-missing and all-invalid inputs produce a useful no-data report.
A measured zero remains valid.
Duplicate timestamps across distinct sensor IDs are handled by the stated identity rule.
Changing row order either preserves a valid summary or produces a documented ordering issue.
extensions: Add a schema-version migration exercise.
Compare two experimental runs using identical validation rules.
Add a human-reviewed quality flag without overwriting the original value.
portfolio: Before/after figures with the raw evidence preserved.
A short explanation of one rejected assumption.
Tests crossing the full read-validate-summarize-write path.
constraints: Use invented or shareable data only.
Do not label thresholds as life-support operating limits.
Do not infer sensor accuracy from observed sample spread alone.

projects.title: Cooling-model verification notebook
projects.summary: Compare an exact first-order model, a numerical ODE solution, and an optional benign cooling experiment, while keeping software error separate from model error.

milestones.title: Write the mathematical contract
milestones.deliverable: A one-state equation, units, initial condition, positive time constant, and assumption list.
milestones.acceptance: The derivative has temperature-per-time units and the equilibrium case is stated before coding.

milestones.title: Verify the implementation
milestones.deliverable: Exact and solve_ivp solutions plotted together for several positive time constants.
milestones.acceptance: Solver success is checked and maximum difference from the exact solution is reported over the same times.

milestones.title: Study numerical choices
milestones.deliverable: A table comparing Euler step sizes and a tighter adaptive-solver configuration.
milestones.acceptance: The table includes exact reference values and distinguishes discretization behavior from physical truth.

milestones.title: Evaluate model limitations
milestones.deliverable: A report explaining spatial gradients, changing ambient conditions, and parameter uncertainty; optionally compare a safe room-temperature object’s measured log.
milestones.acceptance: No measurement is presented as evidence until acquisition conditions and units are documented. Disagreement is investigated rather than hidden by tuning.

testPlan: Equal initial and ambient temperatures remain constant.
Invalid nonpositive tau is rejected.
Initial state is reproduced at t=0.
Above-ambient and below-ambient cases approach equilibrium from the correct side.
extensions: Fit tau from a documented benign experiment and evaluate on a separate interval.
Add a piecewise ambient input and explain continuity.
Compare Python and MATLAB implementations against the same exact fixture.
portfolio: Versioned notebook plus a clean-run script.
A paragraph separating numerical verification from physical validation.
constraints: Requires calculus and differential-equation readiness.
The lumped model is educational and is not a spacecraft or habitat thermal design.
Avoid unsafe heating setups; the project works entirely with synthetic data.

projects.title: A calibration and residual workbench
projects.summary: Create a modest calibration tool that records the fitted domain, shows residuals, and refuses to confuse extrapolation with demonstrated accuracy.

milestones.title: Construct known data
milestones.deliverable: A synthetic linear calibration dataset with documented slope, offset, units, and optional seeded noise.
milestones.acceptance: An exact no-noise fixture recovers the known coefficients within numerical tolerance.

milestones.title: Fit and inspect
milestones.deliverable: A least-squares fit, residual plot, and coefficient report with the fitted input interval.
milestones.acceptance: Residual sign and loss definition are documented; the design matrix columns are explained.

milestones.title: Evaluate beyond the fitting rows
milestones.deliverable: A held-out synthetic set or independent benign dataset, with an evaluation plan written first.
milestones.acceptance: Training and evaluation metrics are labeled separately; the evaluation set is not repeatedly used to tune choices.

milestones.title: Package predictions responsibly
milestones.deliverable: A predictor returning value and domain status, plus a manifest linking coefficients to input data and settings.
milestones.acceptance: Out-of-domain queries are flagged; a missing or invalid model cannot silently yield a default prediction.

testPlan: Exact-line fixture recovers slope and offset.
Constant predictor inputs reveal insufficient information for a unique slope.
Endpoint queries are in-domain.
Out-of-range and non-finite queries follow explicit policies.
extensions: Compare a linear model with a justified alternative.
Study sensitivity to one deliberately changed observation.
Add weighted fitting after learning the statistical meaning of weights.
portfolio: A model card stating domain and limitations.
Tests for predictor behavior at domain boundaries.
constraints: Do not present synthetic uncertainty as instrument certification.
Avoid claiming a confidence interval without defining its assumptions.
Use the simplest model that answers the selected question.

projects.title: An offline robot inspection supervisor
projects.summary: Implement and replay a small supervisory state machine, including stale and missing input, before using a robotics framework.

milestones.title: Specify behavior
milestones.deliverable: A transition table for waiting, ready, inspecting, and review_required, with explicit reset behavior.
milestones.acceptance: Every documented state/event pair has a next state or an explicit ignored-event result.

milestones.title: Build a pure transition core
milestones.deliverable: A function consuming state, event, and timing information and returning a new state plus explanation.
milestones.acceptance: The function performs no sleeping, network calls, or physical I/O and can be tested with fixed values.

milestones.title: Replay challenging sequences
milestones.deliverable: A synthetic event log containing normal progress, missing data, stale data, out-of-order timestamps, and reset attempts.
milestones.acceptance: A written expected state trace is compared against the generated trace for each fixture.

milestones.title: Create an operator-readable report
milestones.deliverable: A timeline showing transitions, event reasons, and the last valid input age.
milestones.acceptance: The report explains why the supervisor requested review and does not automatically resume without the specified event.

testPlan: Start is ignored while waiting.
Missing input during inspection enters review_required.
Age equality obeys the documented stale boundary.
Future timestamps are reported rather than treated as fresh.
Replay results are deterministic and require no wall-clock wait.
extensions: Wrap the core in a ROS 2 node using documentation matching your installed distribution.
Add message sequence identifiers and duplicate handling.
Use recorded simulator output as an adapter while keeping the core unchanged.
portfolio: A short failure analysis for one stale-data scenario.
constraints: This is a desktop behavior exercise, not a controller for physical machinery.
Do not claim hard real-time guarantees.
A robotics framework is optional until the pure logic is understood.

projects.title: A transparent visual marker study
projects.summary: Use small synthetic images and offline photographs to study how a simple brightness-based detector succeeds, fails, and reports ambiguity.

milestones.title: Define image conventions
milestones.deliverable: An input contract for grayscale arrays, value range, axis order, and coordinate output.
milestones.acceptance: A labeled 5×5 fixture has a hand-written mask and expected centroid.

milestones.title: Implement the detector
milestones.deliverable: A threshold mask returning count, centroid, and explicit no-detection status.
milestones.acceptance: No-detection input never divides by zero or returns a fabricated origin coordinate.

milestones.title: Challenge the assumptions

milestones.acceptance: Each fixture has an expected status or a documented limitation; ambiguity is visible in the report.

milestones.title: Report performance honestly
milestones.deliverable: A gallery showing inputs, masks, output coordinates, and short failure explanations.
milestones.acceptance: The report distinguishes satisfying a pixel rule from recognizing an object and identifies where a more capable method would be needed.

testPlan: One selected pixel returns its exact position.
No selected pixels returns None and an explicit status.
An asymmetric fixture exposes row/column swaps.
Two separated regions demonstrate a centroid in empty space.
extensions: Study connected components and add a documented selection rule.
Compare an adaptive threshold only after defining an evaluation set.
Read simulator camera exports without linking detections to actuation.

Pixel position is not metric distance without calibration.
No autonomous physical navigation is part of this project.

projects.title: A reproducible engineering study runner
projects.summary: Build a general but small experiment runner that varies parameters, validates each case, records provenance, and compares results across runs.

milestones.title: Choose a benign model
milestones.deliverable: A documented algebraic or thermal model with known units, input domain, and at least one exact reference case.
milestones.acceptance: The model can be independently checked; no operational propulsion or weapon-design parameters are required.

milestones.title: Define a study configuration
milestones.deliverable: A JSON file listing parameter cases, output location, and model version label.
milestones.acceptance: Invalid cases are rejected with reasons; case identifiers are unique and deterministic.

milestones.title: Run and record
milestones.deliverable: A runner producing per-case result records and a manifest with configuration and input identifiers.
milestones.acceptance: A failed case does not masquerade as a successful zero; successful outputs retain their originating parameters.

milestones.title: Compare and communicate
milestones.deliverable: A parameter-response plot and short report stating sensitivity, limitations, and the next measurement that would reduce uncertainty.
milestones.acceptance: The entire study is recreated by one documented command and a tiny fixture passes in a clean environment.

testPlan: Known reference cases match independent answers.

glossary.definition: A combination of values, names, and operators that evaluates to a value.
glossary.example: power_w * duration_s evaluates an energy estimate.

glossary.definition: Binding a name to the result of an expression at that moment.
glossary.example: Changing power_w later does not automatically recompute energy_j.

glossary.definition: A statement of accepted inputs, output meaning, and failure behavior.
glossary.example: A mean function accepts a nonempty list of finite measurements.

glossary.definition: An input at the edge of a rule or allowed domain.
glossary.example: A value exactly equal to a strict review threshold.

glossary.definition: A value updated repeatedly while processing a collection.
glossary.example: A total mass initialized to zero before a component loop.

glossary.definition: A function whose result depends on its inputs and which does not change external state.
glossary.example: A unit converter that returns a number without reading files.

glossary.definition: A shared description of record fields, types, units, and validity rules.
glossary.example: A telemetry row requires sensor_id, time_s, and temperature_c.

glossary.definition: Information connecting a result to its source data, configuration, and transformations.
glossary.example: A report records its input hash and threshold setting.

glossary.definition: A runtime signal that normal execution cannot continue under current assumptions.
glossary.example: ValueError reports an invalid numeric field.

glossary.definition: A test preserving the expected behavior of a previously failing case.
glossary.example: A one-item list test prevents a last-item omission bug from returning.

glossary.definition: A project-specific Python environment that isolates installed packages from other projects.
glossary.example: A numerical study uses its own .venv and dependency record.

glossary.definition: The number of elements along each array axis.
glossary.example: A (100,3) array might contain 100 samples and three channels.

glossary.definition: Rules allowing compatible array shapes to participate in element-wise operations.
glossary.example: A three-channel offset vector is added to every sample row.

glossary.definition: An array object that shares underlying data with another array.
glossary.example: Editing a basic slice can change the original measurements.

glossary.definition: A difference between an observed or required value and a model result, with a stated sign convention.
glossary.example: Measured temperature minus predicted temperature.

glossary.definition: How sensitive a mathematical problem’s solution is to changes in its inputs.
glossary.example: Nearly dependent equations can strongly amplify small measurement changes.

glossary.definition: Approximation error introduced by representing a continuous problem with finite steps or samples.
glossary.example: A coarse Euler integration differs from an exact cooling curve.

glossary.definition: Checking whether a model or result is suitable for its intended real-world use; in input handling, checking data against a contract.
glossary.example: Comparing a verified cooling implementation against documented measurements tests physical suitability.

glossary.definition: Predicting outside the input range supported by the fitting observations.
glossary.example: Using a calibration measured from 0 to 2 units at an input of 5.

glossary.definition: A timestamp convention with a particular origin and rate.
glossary.example: Seconds since device boot cannot be directly subtracted from Unix wall-clock seconds.

glossary.definition: A source file after preprocessing, compiled as one unit.
glossary.example: telemetry.cpp plus the headers it includes.

glossary.definition: A build tool that connects compiled definitions and libraries.
glossary.example: An unresolved function can compile at the call site yet fail at linking.

glossary.definition: Resource ownership tied to an object lifetime so destruction releases it.
glossary.example: A local ifstream closes its file when it leaves scope.

glossary.definition: An object behaves as an independent value under its documented copy and assignment operations.
glossary.example: Copying a vector produces a separate owned sequence.

glossary.definition: An alias to an existing object; it does not inherently own that object.
glossary.example: const Sample& allows reading a caller-owned record.

glossary.definition: The interval during which an object exists and can be validly used.
glossary.example: A pointer to a local string is invalid after that string is destroyed.

glossary.definition: A condition a component promises to preserve at its interface boundaries.
glossary.example: A bounded queue never contains more than its capacity.

glossary.definition: A collection change makes a previously obtained iterator unusable.
glossary.example: Vector reallocation invalidates iterators into old storage.

glossary.definition: An operation for which the language imposes no requirements on resulting program behavior.
glossary.example: Out-of-bounds vector indexing is not legitimized by one successful run.

glossary.definition: A type holding either a value or no value.
glossary.example: An empty dataset returns no mean instead of a numeric zero.
