glossary.example: A stale check defines units, clock, and equality policy.

glossary.definition: A clock intended for elapsed-time measurement without going backward.
glossary.example: steady_clock measures a local processing interval.

glossary.definition: A mechanism that slows or stops production when downstream work cannot keep up.
glossary.example: A producer waits for queue space instead of dropping a record.

glossary.definition: Communication policies controlling delivery behavior and compatibility.
glossary.example: A ROS 2 publisher and subscriber need compatible reliability settings.

glossary.definition: A repeatable check preserving the fix for a previously observed defect.
glossary.example: A truncated final record remains in the parser test fixtures.

glossary.definition: An ordered collection of values with a defined shape.
glossary.example: A 1-by-4 row of temperature samples.

glossary.definition: A position used to select an element; MATLAB positions start at one.
glossary.example: temperature_c(1) selects the first reading.

glossary.definition: An array of true/false selections applied to aligned data.
glossary.example: temperature_c>30 flags samples above 30 °C.

glossary.definition: An operation applied to corresponding entries rather than matrix algebra.
glossary.example: speed.^2 squares each speed.

glossary.definition: A row-by-column combination representing linear algebra.
glossary.example: A*x combines unknowns according to equation coefficients.

glossary.definition: The difference remaining when a model or solution is checked against data or equations.
glossary.example: A*x-b checks a linear solve.

glossary.definition: How strongly a problem’s answer responds to small changes in its inputs.
glossary.example: Nearly redundant equations can yield sensitive solutions.

glossary.definition: An allowed difference expressed in the output’s units.
glossary.example: A temperature comparison allowing 1e-6 °C of numerical error.

glossary.definition: An allowed error scaled by a reference magnitude.
glossary.example: rtol*abs(reference) grows with the comparison scale.

glossary.definition: An estimate inside the observed input range using a chosen rule.
glossary.example: A midpoint temperature between two measured times.

glossary.definition: An estimate outside the observed input range.
glossary.example: Predicting 100 s behavior from data ending at 20 s.

glossary.definition: A parameter describing the rate of first-order exponential relaxation.
glossary.example: After one tau, exp(-1) of the original temperature difference remains.

glossary.definition: Ambiguity caused when sampling cannot distinguish different continuous signals.
glossary.example: 10 Hz and 90 Hz cosines can match at 100 Hz sampling.

glossary.definition: Repeated model evaluation over a deliberate set of input choices.
glossary.example: Testing cooling time constants of 20, 30, and 40 s.

glossary.definition: The record connecting results to inputs, code, settings, and assumptions.
glossary.example: A report manifest naming data, code revision, and model parameters.

glossary.definition: A region of storage representing a value with a type and lifetime.
glossary.example: A local double result is an object; a pointer can refer to it.

glossary.definition: A value referring to an object or function, or a null value; it does not carry general bounds or ownership.
glossary.example: const uint8_t *data requires a separate accessible byte count.

glossary.definition: The category determining how long storage exists.
glossary.example: An automatic local ends at block exit; allocated storage ends at release.

glossary.definition: The region of source where a name is visible.
glossary.example: A static local has block scope but program-long storage duration.

glossary.definition: The common conversion of an array expression to a pointer to its first element.
glossary.example: An array parameter does not preserve the original count for sizeof.

glossary.definition: A zero character marking the end of a C string.
glossary.example: ROV needs four bytes when represented as a terminated string.

glossary.definition: The number of elements or bytes available for storage, with the unit explicitly stated.
glossary.example: A four-element ring has capacity 4 regardless of its current count.

glossary.definition: Conversion of smaller integer types before many arithmetic operations.
glossary.example: A uint8_t expression may be evaluated as int before a shift.

glossary.definition: An operation for which the language imposes no requirements on the resulting behavior.
glossary.example: Reading beyond an array is invalid even if no crash occurs.

glossary.definition: The byte ordering of a multi-byte representation.
glossary.example: Bytes 01 02 represent 258 under unsigned big-endian decoding.

glossary.definition: Responsibility for managing and eventually releasing a resource.
glossary.example: An allocation-returning API can transfer one free obligation to the caller.

glossary.definition: Access to storage whose owner remains elsewhere.
glossary.example: A view into caller data is valid only while that data remains alive.

glossary.definition: The ability to be entered again before a previous invocation completes under the stated design.
glossary.example: A parser using one static scratch result may not preserve nested-call results.

glossary.definition: A type qualification used for accesses with special observable behavior; it is not a general lock or atomicity guarantee.
glossary.example: A memory-mapped register needs platform-specific volatile access rules and more.

glossary.definition: A C execution environment without all the hosted startup and library assumptions.
glossary.example: A microcontroller project may require board startup code and a restricted library.

glossary.definition: A program that interprets commands and provides a scripting language.
glossary.example: Bash interprets a quoted path and invokes a program.

glossary.definition: The interface through which a user interacts with a shell.
glossary.example: One terminal application can host Bash or PowerShell.

glossary.definition: One value passed to a command after shell interpretation.
glossary.example: "run one.log" should be one argument.

glossary.definition: Syntax controlling expansion and word boundaries.
glossary.example: "$path" preserves a path containing spaces.

glossary.definition: The default stream a program reads.
glossary.example: A pipeline supplies grep with text on stdin.

glossary.definition: The default stream for ordinary program results.
glossary.example: A count printed for another program to consume.

glossary.definition: A separate stream conventionally used for diagnostics.
glossary.example: A missing-input message sent with >&2.

glossary.definition: A numeric outcome returned by a completed command.
glossary.example: Zero conventionally means success.

glossary.definition: A connection from one command’s stdout to another’s stdin.
glossary.example: grep selects lines before wc counts them.

glossary.definition: A shell or tool pattern matching filenames.
glossary.example: *.log selects a class of names under specified rules.

glossary.definition: A separate shell execution environment with its own variable state.
glossary.example: A loop in a pipeline may not update a parent counter.

glossary.definition: A structured sequence of separate values in Bash.
glossary.example: An array holds paths without joining them into one string.

glossary.definition: The current editable files in a Git repository.
glossary.example: A script change appears here before it is staged.

glossary.definition: The selected snapshot prepared for the next Git commit.
glossary.example: git diff --cached shows staged changes.

glossary.definition: The property that repeating an operation has the same intended effect as doing it once.
glossary.example: A validated directory-creation step can tolerate reruns, while blind log appending may duplicate records.

resources.title: CS50’s Introduction to Programming with Python
resources.cost: Free course; optional paid edX certificate
resources.reason: A structured first course covering functions, files, exceptions, tests and debugging, with substantial practice.
resources.usage: Make this your main path. Finish each problem set yourself before moving on; adapt the final project into a telemetry analyzer.

resources.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd edition
resources.reason: A readable alternative to video lessons, with exercises and complete projects.
resources.usage: Use Part I for fundamentals and the data-visualization project for engineering plots. Choose this or CS50P as the main spine, not two full parallel curricula.

resources.title: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python
resources.cost: Free online text; paid print/ebook and optional video course
resources.reason: Makes coding useful immediately through file processing and repetitive work.
resources.usage: After functions and loops, automate organizing simulation outputs or extracting measurements from CSV files.

resources.title: NumPy learning resources
resources.reason: Arrays and vectorized calculations are the foundation of scientific Python.
resources.usage: Start with the absolute-basics tutorial; learn array shapes, indexing, broadcasting and units before optimizing code.

resources.title: SciPy User Guide
resources.reason: Connects programming to integration, optimization, interpolation, statistics and signal processing.
resources.usage: Read only the chapter your current model needs. Check a numerical result against a simple hand calculation or known solution.

resources.title: The Python Tutorial
resources.reason: Precise explanations of Python’s language and standard-library features.
resources.usage: Use after a beginner course. The official page explicitly assumes basic programming knowledge; it is not the gentlest first lesson.

resources.title: LearnCpp
resources.reason: A detailed, modern C++ path that includes compilation, debugging and good habits from the beginning.
resources.usage: Work through lessons in order and compile the exercises. Learn values, functions, std::string and std::vector before advanced templates.

resources.title: Programming: Principles and Practice Using C++, 3rd edition
resources.reason: A programming foundation by C++’s creator, using contemporary C++20/23.
resources.usage: Choose this as a book-based alternative to LearnCpp. Do the drills, and check the book’s setup guidance for its support library.

resources.title: C++ reference
resources.reason: A detailed lookup for language rules, standard containers and library behavior.
resources.usage: Look up one function at a time; pay attention to the C++ standard version. This is a reference, not a first course.

resources.title: C++ Core Guidelines
resources.provider: Bjarne Stroustrup, Herb Sutter and contributors
resources.reason: Explains resource ownership, interfaces and maintainability—the issues that matter as robotics code grows.
resources.usage: After basic classes, focus on resource management, const correctness and interfaces. Apply one rule to a small project each week.

resources.title: CMake Tutorial
resources.reason: Teaches how to build and link projects that contain multiple source files and libraries.
resources.usage: Use after you can compile a small C++ program. Create a reusable library plus a small executable before entering a ROS workspace.

resources.title: ROS 2 Jazzy tutorials
resources.reason: Applies C++ to nodes, topics, services and robot-software communication.
resources.usage: Use documentation matching your installed ROS distribution. Start with command-line tools, then a C++ publisher/subscriber; do not start here to learn basic C++ syntax.

resources.title: MATLAB Onramp
resources.reason: A short, interactive introduction with coding exercises directly in the browser.
resources.usage: Take this first, then recreate the examples from a blank script with different numbers. The advertised duration is about two hours, not a mastery estimate.

resources.title: MATLAB: A Practical Introduction to Programming and Problem Solving, 6th edition
resources.reason: Begins without assumed programming experience and connects programming constructs with MATLAB’s numerical capabilities.
resources.usage: Read functions, arrays, plots and control flow first. The edition uses R2021a-era examples; check current documentation when interfaces differ.

resources.title: MATLAB Cody
resources.reason: Small coding exercises support frequent practice without requiring a large project.
resources.usage: Do one problem from MATLAB Onramp Practice or Basics on Vectors. Favor clear solutions you can explain over the shortest answer.

resources.title: Numerical Computing with MATLAB
resources.cost: Free electronic chapters and code; paid print edition
resources.reason: Explains numerical methods behind matrix computation, differential equations, interpolation and Fourier analysis.
resources.usage: Pair selected chapters with calculus and linear algebra. Modify the provided programs and study when the result becomes inaccurate.

resources.title: Control Tutorials for MATLAB and Simulink
resources.provider: University of Michigan / Carnegie Mellon contributors
resources.cost: Free tutorials; MATLAB/toolbox access may require a license
resources.reason: Connects code and mathematical models to feedback-control behavior.
resources.usage: Use once differential equations and basic control ideas make sense. Begin with a motor or cruise-control example and explain its assumptions.

resources.title: MATLAB Fundamentals / Online Training Suite
resources.cost: Paid training or qualifying school/organization access
resources.reason: An organized path for data analysis, programming and visualization when guided training helps you stay consistent.
resources.usage: Finish free Onramp first. Check your future institution’s access before buying; broader Online Training Suite courses require subscription or eligible linked access.

resources.title: CS50x — Introduction to Computer Science
resources.cost: Free course; optional paid edX certificate
resources.reason: Builds a mental model of algorithms, memory and data structures through demanding exercises, including C.
resources.usage: Focus initially on the C, arrays, algorithms and memory sections. It is a broader computer-science course, not a complete embedded-C curriculum.

resources.title: C Programming: A Modern Approach, 2nd edition
resources.provider: K. N. King / W. W. Norton
resources.reason: Careful explanations and exercises make pointers, arrays and functions approachable.
resources.usage: Use as your main C book if you prefer step-by-step depth. Its C99 coverage is foundational but not a guide to all later C standards.

resources.title: Beej’s Guide to C Programming
resources.reason: An accessible explanation of C’s practical mechanics and deeper language topics.
resources.usage: Use to reinforce pointers, structs and memory after the first lessons. Write and test your own tiny examples as you read.

resources.title: Effective C, 2nd edition
resources.provider: Robert C. Seacord / No Starch Press
resources.reason: Adds modern C23 coverage and attention to correctness and professional programming practices.
resources.usage: Read after basic C. Check which standard your compiler and embedded project support before using newer language features.

resources.title: C reference
resources.reason: A precise lookup for C types, standard-library functions and version differences.
resources.usage: Check array, string and integer behavior before trusting a low-level routine. Keep C rules separate from superficially similar C++ rules.

resources.title: GCC online documentation
resources.reason: Documents language modes, diagnostics and compiler options used to build and inspect C programs.
resources.usage: Use the manual matching your installed compiler. Learn warning options and debugging settings while building small host-side programs.

resources.title: The Unix Shell
resources.reason: A focused first path through files, directories, pipes, loops and scripts.
resources.usage: Work through the provided data exercises, then repeat the same operations on a practice folder of simulation logs.

resources.title: The Linux Command Line
resources.cost: Free authorized PDF; paid print/ebook editions
resources.reason: A thorough introduction to the terminal and shell scripting that can remain useful for years.
resources.usage: Read small sections while using a real terminal. You do not need to finish the whole book before writing useful scripts.

resources.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education
resources.reason: Connects shell use with Git, debugging, development environments and effective technical work.
resources.usage: Start with the shell and command-line environment lessons, then version control. Apply each lesson to the same engineering project.

resources.title: ShellCheck
resources.reason: Explains common quoting, portability and scripting mistakes while you work.
resources.usage: Check every practice script and read each explanation. Passing ShellCheck does not prove that a script does the intended thing.

resources.title: GNU Bash Reference Manual
resources.provider: GNU / Chet Ramey and Brian Fox
resources.reason: Documents expansion, quoting, redirection, exit statuses and Bash-specific behavior.
resources.usage: Look up one confusing behavior at a time. Learn the difference between Bash syntax and portable sh before sharing scripts.

resources.title: Introduction to Linux (LFS101)
resources.cost: Free training; check separate credential offers
resources.reason: Provides broader Linux context beyond isolated shell commands.
resources.usage: Use if Linux itself feels unfamiliar. Treat it as optional supporting context while Python or C++ remains your primary coding track.
